articles.title: US bombers sent home from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
articles.summary:
Aircraft seen leaving Gloucestershire base following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central London

The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an…

blocks.text: The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.

The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.

Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers flying out of the base in Gloucestershire on Sunday.

A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While ⁠operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our ​assets and forces in ‌real time, we can acknowledge ‌now that all US bombers that were deployed to ‌RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States.”

A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometres) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

The US military still maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.

articles.title: Brazil election: Early count puts Bolsonaro ahead of Lula
articles.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's populist ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, took on incumbent left-wing Lula da Silva in a presidential race. Early results show Bolsonaro in the lead.

image.caption: The early count in the Brazilian presidential election puts Flavio Bolsonaro (left) ahead of Luiz Inacio Lula da SilvaImage: Alexandre Meneghini/Pilar Olivares/REUTERS

blocks.text: Polls have closed in Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva seeking a fourth non-consecutive term and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro seeking to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro.
The early results showed a trend favoring Bolsonaro. With 10% of the ballots processed, he has received 51% of the vote. Lula has 40.8%, according to the court.
Because Brazil uses electronic voting machines, final results are expected to be available within several hours of the polls closing.
Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.

blocks.caption: Long queues of voters were seen in parts of Rio de JaneiroImage: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Lula vows to 'defeat the far right'
The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."
Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.
Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.
"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.

blocks.caption: The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final timeImage: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bolsonaro calls for 'change'

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.
He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.

blocks.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if electedImage: Douglas Shineidr/AFP

blocks.text: The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."
"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."
Brazil's 2022 election rematch

The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.

Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."
Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election
The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."
Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."

blocks.caption: US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019]Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance

blocks.text: What happens next?

Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.

In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?

The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.
In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.
Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

articles.title: Polls close in Brazil as Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro remain neck and neck
articles.summary: If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.

blocks.text: Polls have closed in Brazil's general election, after voters queued in long lines for a tight first round of the presidential race.
After casting his ballot, 80-year-old left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva warned that the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".
His challenger, right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".

The result is forecast to be close. BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that the gap between Lula and Bolsonaro is only two points. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.
According to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE), more than 158.7 million Brazilians, including one million people abroad, are eligible to vote in the election.
Lula is challenged by 11 candidates, although BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that candidates other than Lula and Bolsonaro will get only about 10% of the vote.

The TSE has not set a fixed time for the release of the official results, but they are expected within hours because voting is electronic and experience from previous elections shows that results tend to come quickly.

A victory for Bolsonaro would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's re-election would create problems for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Some countries, from which Brazilians living overseas are able to vote, have already released preliminary vote count data.
In China, Lula won 56.63% of the votes, while Bolsonaro came in second with 31.33%. Lula also won in countries including South Korea, New Zealand and Saudi Arabia.
In Israel, however, Bolsonaro won 74.40% of the valid votes. He also won 71.59% of the valid votes in Japan.
Today's result will also determine the composition of the Senate from February 2027 onwards, as 54 of the Senate's 81 seats are being contested, representing two-thirds of the chamber.
Currently, the largest bloc in the Senate is Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), followed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD), which has served in a coalition government under Lula.

In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father, Jair. But the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.
Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup and is barred from standing for office.
Because of recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has been prohibited from posting on social media or making public statements.
Despite these restrictions, there is little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has his father's backing.

articles.title: Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England
articles.summary:
Shadow chancellor will also promise to scrap affordable homes regulations as part of strategy to refocus on growth

The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including…

blocks.text: The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency.

The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, will say the party intends to “streamline regulations” that protect nature and oblige developers to include affordable homes and community services such as GP surgeries, to speed up infrastructure and housebuilding.
The announcements on Monday are a signal that the party intends to refocus on the economy, an area where it has made relatively little progress in the polls.

blocks.caption: Andrew Griffith arrives on the first day of the Conservative conference in Birmingham on Sunday. He will say the party intends to ‘streamline regulations’.  Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA

blocks.text: Tory strategists believe there is a major opening to make gains against Reform and Labour, given the limited focus on growth from Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, at the Labour conference last week.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, published a new tract on Sunday called The Right Way, which she said would be the bedrock that underpinned the party’s policy development before the next election. Polls have the party still trailing third behind Labour and Reform UK.

Introducing the document – inspired by Margaret Thatcher’s The Right Approach from 1976 – Badenoch said the Conservatives still expected to win the next election and needed to “hit the ground running … We will need to be ready from day one, having already shown people what kind of government we are going to be.”

“Keir Starmer didn’t have a plan. That’s why he’s gone,” she said. “Andy Burnham doesn’t have one either and that is why I know the announcements he is making will all come to naught. We have to be different, different from Labour, and different from the party we were two years ago.”

In a slew of announcements at the Conservative party conference on Monday, the Tories will pledge measures that they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,0000, including scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding, such as the Future Homes Standard, which requires all new homes in England to be zero-carbon ready.

The party will promise to replace section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy that oblige developers to build a proportion of affordable housing and support school and health service demands locally. Instead, there will be a “one stop” levy on developers, Griffith will say.
The party has also pledged to abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency, “moving to a more streamlined regulatory landscape to protect our environment”.

Griffith will say in his first speech as shadow chancellor that the Tories would continue to back the expansion of Heathrow airport and leave the Aarhus convention, which makes it easier for community groups to oppose developments.
Conservative shadow Treasury ministers will be tasked with finding new ways of simplifying tax for individuals and businesses, Griffith will say, calling the tax code “a cat’s cradle of complexity”.
after newsletter promotion
In his speech, he will say: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation.

“Our task just got bigger. We face a prime minister that wants to return Britain to an imagined past. A socialist fever dream of the 1970s. Cheaper homes, lower taxes and less red tape. This will be the most ambitious deregulation project in a generation. We will be more prepared than ever before. We will set out our plans line by line. Every bill, every regulation, every chapter.”

Griffith will say that the government must speed up the building of a Heathrow third runway in whatever way it can. “I refuse to accept for a single moment that the country of Brunel and Bazalgette, of the vaccine taskforce and the Mulberry harbours, has to sit around waiting until the 2040s to get a third runway built,” he will say.
Burnham has recently expressed personal scepticism about the Heathrow third runway, saying he would take differing views seriously.
The new shadow housing secretary, Katie Lam, will say the scrapping of housing regulations and of enforcement bodies would mean “anti-growth ideologues can never again hold our country hostage”.

The party said Natural England and the Environment Agency were preventing too many homes being built and adding unnecessary costs to building. Both bodies would be scrapped, with their necessary functions brought directly into Defra.

articles.title: Chinese ships, planes block PH operations
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Sunday criticized the China Coast Guard (CCG) for reportedly stopping them from going after foreign vessels suspected of engaging in dynamite fishing near Pag-asa…

blocks.text: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Sunday criticized the China Coast Guard (CCG) for reportedly stopping them from going after foreign vessels suspected of engaging in dynamite fishing near Pag-asa Island.

At the same time, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said that two Chinese aircraft repeatedly maneuvered close to a Philippine military aircraft conducting a routine maritime patrol over Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal) in the West Philippine Sea, putting the Filipino crew in danger.

“At around [7:20 a.m. on Sunday], personnel of the Joint Task Unit Pag-asa saw a foreign fishing vessel apparently doing blast fishing in the area. [The] Coast Guard District Kalayaan Island Group quickly formed an interagency team. The team deployed PCG High-Speed Response Boat HSRB-019, a Philippine Navy RHIB [rigid hull inflatable boat] and rubber boat, and a PNP Maritime Group RHIB,” the PCG said.
The PCG noted that as the Philippine team left the sheltered port of Pag-asa Island around 9:50 a.m., CCG vessels 5102 and 21581 moved toward them, blasting their horns.

When the Philippine team reached the foreign fishing vessel about 500 meters away from Sandy Cay 2 around 10 a.m., several small boats returned to the mother ship. The foreign vessel then moved away, ignoring the Filipinos’ orders for it to stop.
The PCG reported that CCG 21581 blocked and shadowed the Philippine team as it was following the foreign vessel and even came within about 10 yards of the PCG boat.
This prompted the Filipinos to stop following the foreign ship and return to Pag-asa Island around 10:48 a.m. “for safety reasons.”
The PCG condemned the incident, noting that dynamite fishing is prohibited under the Philippine Fisheries Code.

“The PCG stresses that this was a routine law enforcement operation against an illegal and destructive practice. It was not directed at any country. The incident will be documented and referred through the Department of Foreign Affairs for appropriate action through existing channels,” it said.

It added that the CCG “has no law enforcement authority in the territorial sea of Pag-asa Island. By obstructing Philippine authorities, the CCG did not protect the marine environment. It made it easier for a suspected violator to escape.”

In the second incident, two Chinese aircraft repeatedly maneuvered close to a Philippine military aircraft conducting a routine maritime patrol over Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal) in the West Philippine Sea, endangering the Filipino crew.
In a statement on Sunday, the AFP confirmed that its Air Force C-208 utility turboprop encountered two Chinese military planes, including a J-16 fighter, while flying over the shoal on Oct. 3.

“During the encounter, the J-16 repeatedly approached and maneuvered in close proximity to the Philippine aircraft, including maneuvering ahead of and around it and positioning itself within the Philippine aircraft’s wake,” the AFP said. “These maneuvers posed an aviation safety risk.”
No personnel was hurt during the close encounter, and the AFP aircraft was able to “safely complete its assigned maritime patrol and return without further incident.”
Within EEZ
Bajo de Masinloc, also known as Panatag Shoal, is a traditional fishing ground located 230 kilometers (124 nautical miles) west of Luzon, and 830 km (448 NM) from mainland China.
Under the 2016 arbitral award, it is classified as a rock that generates only a 12-nm territorial sea, with no entitlement to an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) or continental shelf.
Its surrounding waters thus lie within the Philippines’ EEZ, extending 370 km (200 NM) from its baselines, granting the Philippines sovereign rights over living and nonliving resources.
However, the shoal has been under China’s control since 2012.
According to the AFP, the latest incident was part of a “recurring pattern of unsafe and coercive behavior” against Philippine government vessels and aircraft conducting lawful operations.
“The AFP remains vigilant and will continue to prioritize the safety of its personnel and aircraft while carrying out its mandate,” it said. INQ
For comprehensive coverage, in-depth analysis, visit our special page for West Philippine Sea updates. Stay informed with articles, videos, and expert opinions.

articles.title: Bosnian Serb nationalist Dodik declares party victory in Bosnia election
articles.summary:
Staunchly pro-Russia politician has dominated campaign and inflamed divisions despite not appearing on ballot

Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his…

blocks.text: Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992-95 war.

Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that has sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia.

Formerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war.

With nearly 90% of votes counted, Dodik’s ally Željka Cvijanović of the rightwing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats had more than 55% of the votes to take one of the three seats in the country’s tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by about 30 percentage points.

Speaking at a news conference late on Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a “vast majority” in Republika Srpska’s assembly, and credited US president Donald Trump’s “magnificent victory” in 2024 and Russian president Vladimir Putin’s support for the election win.
“No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said. “We will not give up, but continue for our people … I cannot believe that we smashed it like this.”

About 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country’s multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.

With more than 94% of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipović of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while the incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency, Denis Bećirović of the Social Democratic party, led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegović, by fewer than three percentage points.
Both Filipović and Bećirović declared victory in their races late on Sunday before all votes were counted.
Bosnia’s central election commission said that 1,432,269 votes were cast in total, a turnout of 42% that was down by about 8% from Bosnia’s last election in 2022.

Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war.
Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia’s national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country.
At his party’s final election rally on Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska’s administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia “is dead”.
after newsletter promotion
“It is an impossible country. It doesn’t make any sense,” Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian ambassador Igor Khalabukov.

Such political and ethnic divisions – in which the country’s Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines – have blocked Bosnia’s progress toward joining the EU despite the bloc’s efforts to encourage the country’s divided leaders to work together for reform.
Dragan Bursać, an analyst, said that despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he “is still in command. He is everywhere.”
“It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them,” Bursać said.

One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades on from the war, which started in 1992 after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.

Bosnia’s wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladić, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.

articles.title: 'This is home for me': Amber Marshall reflects as 20th season of Heartland set to begin
articles.summary: Amber Marshall has grown up on Heartland, the long-running CBC drama that mirrors her real-life love of horses and ranch life. As the show celebrates its 20th season, its cast, characters and global…

image.caption: A young Amber Marshall learns how to ride a horse. (Submitted by Amber Marshall)

blocks.text: Heartland star Amber Marshall is an Alberta ranch girl in real life, too
For nearly 20 years, Amber Marshall has lived, in some ways, the life of Amy Fleming.
She was 19 when she began playing the horse-loving teenager at the centre of Heartland, the CBC drama about a family ranch in the Alberta Foothills.
Marshall has been riding since she was five, got her first horse at 10 and had long imagined a future surrounded by animals.
"I knew that that's who I wanted to be when I grew up," Marshall, now 38, told CBC's Ian Hanomansing in a new interview. "I wanted to be Amy Fleming."
Nearly two decades later, the distinction between actor and character has become unusually difficult to draw.
Marshall, who is from London, Ont., lives on a ranch of her own. She is surrounded by horses and cows, fosters dogs and has made Alberta her home. She moved there during Heartland’s second season.

items: Heartland's milestone 20th Season: Everything you need to know before the premiere on CBC Gem

blocks.text: "I can never see myself relocating again. This is home for me," she said.
Heartland, which begins its 20th season on Sunday, is the longest-running scripted drama in Canadian television history.

Based on the books by Lauren Brooke, it began airing in 2007 and has grown from a Canadian family series into an international phenomenon — with viewers in countries ranging from England and France to Australia and the United States.
The series follows Amy and her family as they work to keep their ranch operating while navigating growing up, relationships, grief and financial pressures.

Amy has married, become a mother and been widowed following the sudden death of her husband, Ty Borden (Graham Wardle). Her sister, Lou (Michelle Morgan), has built a career and raised a family, while their grandfather Jack (Shaun Johnston) has remained the family patriarch.
The characters have aged and changed, allowing viewers to grow up with them.

items: Heartland's youngest stars: The twins who play Lyndy grow up on the show

blocks.text: Marshall has met fans who were babies when the show began and have followed it through childhood and adolescence.
Some have told her that Heartland helped them through difficult periods in their lives.

"It’s special to know that a show can resonate with someone who's never been to Canada, that's never been to Alberta," she said, "and they can watch it and feel a connection to those characters and to that Heartland family."
A family story that resonates beyond Alberta
That connection was on display at a fan event in Alberta on Aug. 11, when viewers travelled from all over the globe.

Sarah Metcalf and her daughter, Riva, came from Manchester, England. Riva first encountered Heartland through a schoolbook when she was nine, then began watching the series after relatives in Canada sent the family DVDs.

"We watched one episode and it would leave on a cliffhanger, and then you'd have to watch the next one," Sarah said. "It’s a very special series, and we're very lucky that we came across it.... It’s a special part of us."

Leanne and Ayla Gale travelled from Brisbane, Australia. Ayla says the show’s performances and cinematography inspired her own interest in film, while her mother, Leanne, was drawn to the Alberta scenery. "I love Canada. I love the Rockies, the scenery, the mountains, pine trees, ranches,” Leanne said.
Marshall agrees that the landscape is central to the show. "The Heartland vista has become a character of its own," she said.
Fans often ask whether the Foothills are real or the product of green-screen effects. Marshall said they are and that the scenery has inspired some viewers to visit Alberta.
"It’s just a beautiful part of Canada," she said. "People want to feel and experience what they see on TV, and I don’t think they’re disappointed."

items: Heartland star Amber Marshall to guest star on Murdoch Mysteries

blocks.text: Marshall said visitors can experience the region’s western lifestyle, nature and "calming presence," becoming fully immersed in the Alberta Foothills.
She told Hanomansing that Alberta’s slower pace has taught her to resist the constant rush she notices when she returns to Ontario.
"I love being able to walk out in the field, say, 'You know what, I probably should be doing something else, but I'm just going to really enjoy this nice day,'" Marshall said.
Horses keep everyone present
That calm has shaped the Heartland set, where horses are central to the production. Marshall said their unpredictability keeps the series realistic and forces the actors to remain present.
"Horses are just living in the moment," she said. "They don't read the script, they don't know what's going on.”
The animals also require a quiet, relaxed workplace.
"You cannot have a tense set with animals and expect them to perform,” she said. "We have to be quiet. We have to be relaxed. We have to be calm."

Marshall's commitment to animals began long before Heartland. As a child, she wanted to become a veterinarian and volunteered at an animal shelter from the age of 10. She now runs the Foothills Animal Support Society, which helps animals and their families who might need access to veterinary care.
She has also spoken out against opening protected areas of the Rocky Mountains to coal mining, saying she has seen the damage caused to landscapes, water sources and animals.
"I do believe that we have a moral obligation to protect this beautiful place," she said.
'I'll do Heartland till I die'
Marshall said she believes Heartland endures because it offers something increasingly rare: wholesome, intergenerational television that leaves viewers feeling better instead of more anxious.
"It makes you feel very complete,” she said. "It makes you feel settled. It makes you feel like you've done something right for your mind and body."
She said the show is not confined to a particular era or stage of life. Its characters can continue to grow as new people arrive, others leave and families change.
As for how many seasons remain, her answer was immediate: "Oh gosh, another 20."
"I’ll do Heartland till I die," she said. "This is my life. I love being in Western Canada. I love being on a ranch. I love being surrounded by my animals."

articles.title: Polls close in Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
articles.summary: Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, the Serb nationalist candidate backed by disqualified secessionist leader Milorad Dodik, took the lead for the Serb seat of the three-member presidency.

image.caption: Preliminary results are expected to be available late Sunday after polls closeImage: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Polls closed in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday evening, with around 3.4 million voters eligible to take part in the Balkan country's general election.
Citizens voted for officials across multiple tiers of government, including members of the multiethnic, tripartite presidency.

With counting underway, Serb nationalist Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist ‌Darijana ​Filipovic each took an early lead in for the presdential seats of their respective ethnicities.

Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik who is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

blocks.caption: Voters queued in Banja Luka and other cities around the countryImage: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.

The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges. There's been an economic slowdown, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and a long-drawn-out political gridlock, with the ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that links them.
The election will see adversary ethnic parties, the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH, pitted against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.
Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results expected to be released late Sunday.
What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, two semi-autonomous entities, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district.
Both entities are further split into several cantons and communities.

The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war which was triggered by the breakup of Yugoslavia.
Simmering ethnic tensions
Currently in Bosnia and Herzegovina's populace, around half are Muslim Bosniaks, while 31% are Orthodox Serb and 15% are Catholic Croat.
The country has been peaceful in recent years but its ethnonationalist parties have kept the divisions alive even as voters say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric and division.
Milorad Dodik not on the ballot but still dominant in Republika Srpska
In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remains the key figure despite not being on the ballot.

Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
Dodik-backed Savo Minic is running for the Republika Srpska's presidency.
Dodik wants close ‌ties with Serbia and Russia. He has just returned from Moscow where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.
What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.
The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.
Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.
Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
EU ambitions
Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.
But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws.
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028

articles.title: Brazil presidential election 2026: first-round live results
articles.summary:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of the presidential race

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son…

blocks.text: The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a military coup. The president in Brazil is directly elected, and candidates need more than 50% of the vote to avoid a second round. Polls close at 17.00 BRT / 21.00 BST.
Live first round results
Guardian graphic. Source: TES
How the election works

Brazil’s president is directly elected: each voter’s ballot counts equally and there is no electoral college. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the valid votes cast in the first round, a second runoff election will be held three weeks later between the two candidates who polled highest.

According to opinion polls, there are two leading candidates. The first is the incumbent president, Lula, 80, a veteran of the Brazilian left who has served three terms. During his first two terms, between 2003 and 2011, he was credited with overseeing a historic period of commodity-fuelled growth and poverty reduction.

Brazilian presidents are limited to two consecutive terms, so if he wins this time he will not be able to stand in 2030. In 2018 Lula was jailed on corruption charges, although his conviction was quashed after 580 days behind bars.

Lula’s principal opponent is the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison. Flávio is a 45-year-old lawyer and a former senator from Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election but has endorsed his son’s campaign and hopes to regain his freedom if he wins.

Opinion polls suggest no other candidate will come close to the two frontrunners, but neither is there a clear leader in polling for the 25 October runoff. The new leader will take power on 5 January 2027.

One of the most important states to watch is Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, and is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing in Minas. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate there by more than 1.7m votes and was elected president.
Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000 and also won the nationwide race. History suggests that whoever wins Minas, will win the election.

articles.title: Pakistan: Imran Khan supporters demand ex-PM's release
articles.summary: Thousands of Imran Khan supporters have begun a trek to Islamabad to demand he be freed as Pakistan's political leadership remains in deadlock. The government has set up roadblocks to keep protesters…

image.caption: Imran Khan's supporters hope to inspire hundreds of thousands of Pakistanis to get behind the ex-PM's cause Image: Maaz Awan/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of Imran Khan supporters began to make their way to the Pakistani capital Islamabad on Sunday as a slow moving convoy set off on an 80-kilometer (50-mile) trip that will take several days to complete.
Some 5,000 supporters are traveling by bus, car and truck from northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party (PTI) holds power.

March organizers say they intend to rally hundreds of thousands of supporters to Khan's cause along the way, hoping to bring about his release from prison as well as his transfer to a hospital where he can receive medical treatment and regular visits from his family.
Government officials say Khan is in no need of hospitalization and that he receives regular visits already.
In August, Pakistan's Supreme Court ruled that he should be moved to a civilian hospital but authorities returned him to prison after a short stay at a government-run medical facility.

blocks.caption: Several rallies will be held along the journey to IslamabadImage: Maaz Awan/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Imran Khan still very influential despite being behind bars for years

Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence inside Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.

Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, left office in April 2022, when he lost a no-confidence vote. He has been in prison since August 2023. Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023.
Moreover, his supporters say the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.

Speaking with AFP news agency, James Dorsey of the National University of Singapore called Khan "a populist leader" with "a genuine popular movement that has broad popular support," adding, "That's why I think you've seen the determination by the government to prevent (protesters) from entering Islamabad."

Dorsey noted that in his opinion, security concerns — particularly those stemming from Pakistan's unresolved February 2026 war with Afghanistan — would likely force Islamabad to avoid escalation in the face of protests.
The march, he says, is "a problem for the government, but I don't think it's an existential threat."

blocks.caption: Organizers say the march will grow from 5,000 supporters as they advance toward Islamabad this week  Image: Maaz Awan/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistan's government accuses Khan supporters of having terrorist sympathies

The march was initially set to commence on September 27, but organizers postponed it amid talks aimed at finding a political solution to the standoff between the government of Prime Minister Shebaz Sharif and Imran Khan's PTI — and despite the government erecting massive roadblocks in and around Islamabad.
The march began after those talks failed.
PTI Chairman Gohar Khan on Sunday said negotiations to stave off the march had remained deadlocked after two rounds of talks.
Khan's supporters now plan to hold rallies at a series of overnight stops during what will likely be a four or five day march.

Speaking from atop a large truck, the trailer of which is emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, provincial chief minister Sohail Afridi said the movement will bring Pakistan's political standoff to the heart of the capital.
Why Pakistan is fighting the Taliban it once backed
Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the breakdown in negotiations, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the march.
In the past, protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent, including in 2024, when security personnel and civilians were killed.
Pakistan has also seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government cited these as reason for delaying the march.

The government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks. The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

articles.title: Nearly all women arriving on small boats have been raped, says Shabana Mahmood
articles.summary:
Home secretary warns people traffickers will exploit asylum seekers because they decide who comes to the UK

Nearly all women who try to reach the UK in small boats from northern France have…

blocks.text: Nearly all women who try to reach the UK in small boats from northern France have been raped on their journey, Shabana Mahmood has claimed.
In an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast, the home secretary said far-right, balaclava-wearing activists would “kill” or “kick me out of my own country” if they took power.

Speaking to the former Tory minister Rory Stewart and Tony Blair’s former close adviser Alastair Campbell, she said sexual abusers would exploit most asylum seekers as long as traffickers continued to decide who came to the UK.

She said: “We’re not in control of this border. The sifting of the people that end up in the north of France and are about to get on a dinghy is done by criminal gangs who are also, by the way, people traffickers.

“You can almost guarantee that every woman that’s in the north of France has probably been raped along the journey. Some of the men too, they’ve certainly been abused and threatened. That is not the model that should decide whether somebody gets to come to the UK, make this their place of sanctuary and ultimately become one of us.”

blocks.caption: Shabana Mahmood said she was ‘very uncomfortable’ about the arrests of 82 people at the Labour conference for displaying articles in support of Palestine Action. Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Asked by Campbell about balaclava-wearing protesters shutting down ports and praising her policies, she said they should “sod off”.

She added: “They’re just troublemakers. You know, they’d kill me in a minute if they could, and they’d definitely kick me out of my own country. So let’s just be really clear about who and what they are. They don’t think I’m a true Brit and they hate the fact that I’m a Muslim.”
Mahmood also said she considered herself “part of the pro-Palestinian cause” and felt “very uncomfortable” over the arrests of activists opposing the ban imposed on Palestine Action.
Merseyside police arrested 82 people on Monday at the Labour party conference on suspicion of wearing or carrying articles supporting a proscribed organisation.
In a protest organised by Defend Our Juries, scores of people sat outside the conference centre in Liverpool, many holding handmade banners saying they supported Palestine Action.
after newsletter promotion

Mahmood said: “For those of us who have been in the pro-Palestinian cause all of our lives, these are people – sometimes you’ll know who they are, you know, you’ve been on the marches with them – it feels very uncomfortable to see them falling foul of section 13 of the Terrorism Act.”

However, she defended enforcing the ban, regardless of her views: “You’ve got to be able to apply your principles, even when it’s uncomfortable for you, because you’re going to really want to apply them when it’s something you, you know, with your whole heart, are feeling very passionately about.”

Authorities were preparing on Sunday for the arrival of a migrant dinghy heading for the south coast. The boat was being shadowed by French coastguard and rescue vessels and moving toward the Channel boundary line, according to ship tracking data.
It appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning.

Caroline Dinenage, the Conservative MP for Gosport in Hampshire, said there was “nothing to suggest” the boat would land on the county’s coast but police were “making preparations should that situation change”.

A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.”

Imran Hussain, a director at the Refugee Council, welcomed the home secretary’s acknowledgment of widespread sexual violence, but questioned why the government had closed safe and legal routes which could help asylum seekers avoid falling into the hands of predators.

“We know from our services that women and girls fleeing war and persecution face sexual violence both in the conflicts they have escaped and on the journeys they are forced to make in search of safety,” he said.

“That is why in welcoming the government’s announcement last week of new safe routes we called for them not to be limited to a few hundred people. Last year the government closed family reunion, the safe route for refugees which overwhelmingly benefits women and children.

“It is entirely right to talk about the dangers women face on these journeys but we should not be closing the safe routes that could keep them out of harm’s way. Protecting women means more safe routes, not fewer.”

articles.title: AFP says Chinese J-16 fighter flew too close to PH aircraft over Bajo de Masinloc
articles.summary: An AFP aircraft encountered two Chinese military aircraft during a routine patrol over Bajo de Masinloc, with at least one of the Chinese planes flying too close in an "unsafe" manner.

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 1:44am

An Armed Forces of the Philippines aircraft encountered two Chinese military aircraft during a routine patrol over the West Philippine Sea, with at least one of the Chinese planes flying too close in an "unsafe" manner.
In a statement on Sunday, AFP Public Affairs Office Chief Colonel Xerxes Trinidad said that the incident occurred on Saturday, October 3.

"[A]n AFP C-208 aircraft conducting a routine maritime patrol over the vicinity of Bajo de Masinloc encountered two Chinese military aircraft on 03 October 2026. One of the aircraft was identified as a J-16 fighter aircraft," he said.

"During the encounter, the J-16 repeatedly approached and maneuvered in close proximity to the Philippine aircraft, including maneuvering ahead of and around it and positioning itself within the Philippine aircraft’s wake. These maneuvers posed an aviation safety risk."

Trinidad said that the AFP aircraft was able to complete its patrol and return without incident. However, he said that the incident was "part of a recurring pattern of unsafe and coercive behavior against Philippine government vessels and aircraft conducting lawful operations."

Trinidad said that the AFP will continue to conduct routine maritime and air patrols in the West Philippine Sea. "The AFP remains vigilant and will continue to prioritize the safety of its personnel and aircraft while carrying out its mandate," he added.
Also on Sunday, Chinese vessels obstructed a law enforcement operation against a foreign fishing vessel suspected of dynamite fishing near Pag-asa Island.

The operation involved personnel from the Philippine Coast Guard, the Philippine Navy and the Philippine National Police Maritime Group responding to a report of suspected blast fishing near Sandy Cays 2 and 3, about three nautical miles west of Pag-asa.

The PCG said two China Coast Guard vessels sounded their horns, radio-challenged the Philippine team and later shadowed and blocked its boats. A People's Liberation Army Navy helicopter also circled above the Philippine personnel four times. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere?
articles.summary: A new report says the AI model Claude was used in pro-Russian campaigns in the Central African Republic. Similar allegations have been made about propaganda in Democratic Republic of the Congo,…

image.caption: The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agentsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled "Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported.

The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary group Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world.
Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition

The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.

blocks.caption: According to Anthropic, Russia is using AI in African countries to spread its messagesImage: Fred de Noyelle/Godong/picture alliance

blocks.text: Lou Osborn, a member of All Eyes on Wagner, was involved in the research for the latest report. He believes these methods are part of a practice that has already been observed in connection with the Wagner Group in the Central African Republic. "There have been several arrests of people who were not necessarily closely affiliated with the Touadera regime," he told DW. "They’ve been doing this for several years now."Faustin-Archange Touadera has been president of the Central African Republic since 2016.

"The arrests were the subject of online campaigns in newspapers and on the radio which portrayed those individuals either as proxies for France or Western intelligence services, or as people preparing a coup against Touadera," Osborn added.

Anthropic also reported that Claude was prompted to portray opposition figures as armed militants in an effort to provoke security forces into taking action against them. Anthropic says Claude refused the request. However, the report did not name the opposition figures who were monitored, specify the exact nature of the data collected, or say who received it.
'The government wants to get rid of us,' opposition says

For the opposition, the Anthropic report underscored the determination of the government in Bangui and its Russian allies to get rid of them. Martin Ziguele, chairman of the Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People, referred to an earlier case. "We have been observing this since 2020, when the CPC, a coalition of rebel groups, attacked Bangui. Strangely enough, several media outlets did everything in their power to establish alleged links between certain opposition leaders and the CPC," Ziguele told DW.

"There were also attacks against the opposition claiming that we were being paid by foreign countries. There was an attempt to pass a law stating that foreign agents were present in the country. All of this relates to the activities of the Wagner Group, as does this latest revelation."

blocks.caption: An arial view of Bangui, Central African RepublicImage: Sam Mednick/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: DW also sought a statement from Russia. "Yes, I heard about [the report] in the news," said Dmitri Sytyi, a representative of the Russian mission in the Central African Republic. "But there are no concrete facts in it. [...] These are vague allegations, without precision and without evidence."
AI influence operations across the DRC, Kenya, Sudan and Mali?

Russia firmly denies the allegations, but the report indicates that the Central African Republic was not an isolated case. According to the report, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya, Sudan and Mali were also affected.

In the DRC, Anthropic identified 318 articles that, according to the report, were published by a network of about 70 fake news sites and subsequently distributed by more than 250 fictitious accounts on X. The content supported the positions of the Congolese government against the backdrop of the conflict with Rwanda.
In Kenya, Claude was allegedly used to generate batches of 50 messages at a time that supported the government and were hostile toward the opposition.

blocks.caption: Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario AmodeiImage: Don Feria/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Sudan, Anthropic says AI was used as part of an operation attributed to individuals in the United Arab Emirates — particularly to create fabricated witness statements for the United Nations.

In Mali, meanwhile, an adviser with ties to intelligence services allegedly used Claude to develop a platform for monitoring telecommunications. According to the report, it was designed to target 25 million SIM cards and circumvent the requirement to obtain judicial authorization.
Anthropic says it uncovered and shut down all of these different operations between December 2025 and August 2026, primarily by deleting the accounts involved and strengthening its detection systems.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says
articles.summary: Pike's lawyer says doctors are still trying to clear two lethal doses of pentobarbital from her body.

blocks.text: US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.
Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.
Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days."
He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors.
He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said.

Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday.

"If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be."

He called on the governor to commute her death sentence to a life sentence "at the very least". "She has endured a torturous attempt at executing her," he said. "She's spent over 30 years in prison, most of that in solitary confinement."
"We don't know right now - and we may never know - what sort of torture she endured during [her failed execution]."
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.
She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez travelled to Nashville for the execution, which moved ahead despite last-minute legal challenges.
Martinez, who supported Pike's death sentence, told local news outlet WJXX that she "broke down in tears" after finding out it was not successful.
"I think that the state owes me a big apology," she said.
The state's Department of Correction has defended the use of lethal injections, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".

Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.

articles.title: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest
articles.summary: The allegations were made after police detained dozens of protesters demanding the resignation of the election chief over changes to voter rolls.

blocks.text: Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.
The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.
Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls.
In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.
The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this".
"Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests.
She said the police were resorting to "brutality".

articles.title: ICC amends e-court protocol ahead of Duterte trial
articles.summary: Less than two months before the start of the crimes against humanity trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the International Criminal Court (ICC) has amended its protocol for digital evidence…

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 12:00am
The International Criminal Court is investigating killings linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte's anti-drug campaign, which rights groups say left thousands dead.
Philstar.com / illustration

MANILA, Philippines — Less than two months before the start of the crimes against humanity trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the International Criminal Court (ICC) has amended its protocol for digital evidence and other information on witnesses and victims.
The ICC Registry, which is in charge of the administrative aspects of the court, submitted last week the amended E-Court Protocol that will be used during Duterte’s trial.

“This Protocol defines the standards according to which the participants should prepare and provide evidence, potential evidence and material in electronic form with the Court,” read the document submitted to the ICC Trial Chamber III.

“Furthermore, this Protocol defines metadata which should accompany the materials submitted. These standards are designed to minimize the document management and technology costs to the participants and the Court and to allow for the efficient management of proceedings,” it added.

Trial judges earlier directed the ICC Registry to submit the amended E-Court Protocol after it granted the prosecution’s request to add a URL (uniform resource locator) metadata field for each of the open source or user-generated evidence submitted in the case.
The prosecution said the additional field will allow parties to easily identify the URL or link “associated with the open source evidence at the time it was captured.”
The judges, however, denied the defense’s request for an additional “expert verification” field to accompany all forms of open source and user-generated evidence.

“The (defense’s) requested amendment, if implemented, requires the Prosecution to prepare additional materials that contain information regarding the relevance and admissibility of open-source and user-generated evidence, before the Defense analyses evidence and raises any abovementioned issues,” read the Sept. 26 decision.
Defense lawyer Peter Haynes argued that there is a need for extra caution to ensure that evidence is properly verified before it is submitted to the court.
But the ICC prosecutor said adding a separate expert verification field is “unreasonable, unnecessary and against the interests of judicial efficiency.”

articles.title: PCG commandant’s term should not be extended – DOJ
articles.summary: The three-year term of Philippine Coast Guard commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan should no longer be extended even through reappointment or temporary designation by President Marcos, the Department…

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The three-year term of Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan should no longer be extended even through reappointment or temporary designation by President Marcos, the Department of Justice (DOJ) has declared.

“It is the opinion of this Department that Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan’s three-year maximum term as PCG Commandant, which began on 19 October 2023, expires on 19 October 2026 and may not be extended through executive action,” the three-page DOJ Legal Opinion No. 23 issued on Sept. 17 stated.

The agency came up with its opinion following a request from Presidential Management Staff Secretary Elaine Masukat about “whether the three-year term of the Commandant of the Philippine Coast Guard may be extended.”

Citing Republic Act 9993 that created the PCG in 2009 and amended by RA 12122, the opinion signed by Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida maintains “the statutory language is clear… (and the) three-year period is expressly prescribed as the ‘maximum term.’ ”
It added the PCG law’s provision on the commandant’s three-year maximum term of office cannot be “circumvented through another form of executive action, such as reappointment.”

Moreover, a possible temporary designation “to address a vacancy in accordance with the law… cannot be invoked to allow Admiral Gavan to continue occupying beyond the three-year maximum prescribed” by the PCG law.

articles.title: Dropping VP bribery charges may be shortchanging Filipinos – Palace
articles.summary: Malacañang yesterday questioned whether the House prosecution panel would be shortchanging the Filipino public if it decides to drop the bribery charges against Vice President Sara Duterte in…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 5, 2026 | 12:00am

While acknowledging that trial strategy rests entirely with the House prosecutors, Presidential Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro pointed out that the inclusion of the bribery allegation in the Articles of Impeachment meant the panel had sufficient evidence to back it up before the Senate impeachment court.
The Philippine STAR / Noel Pabalate

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang yesterday questioned whether the House prosecution panel would be shortchanging the Filipino public if it decides to drop the bribery charges against Vice President Sara Duterte in her ongoing impeachment trial.

“If they back out of the bribery charges against the Vice President, wouldn’t the Filipino people who want to know the whole truth be shortchanged or put at a disadvantage? Again, the decision is theirs,” Castro told reporters.
‘Trillanes was not blocked’
Meanwhile, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian defended impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero over the non-issuance of a subpoena to former senator Antonio Trillanes IV.

Speaking to radio dzBB, Gatchalian said senator-judges were consulted on the matter while noting that Trillanes’ recent financial allegations could still serve as “leads” when government regulators take the stand this week in the impeachment trial.
He also pushed back against Trillanes’ claim that Escudero single-handedly blocked him from testifying in the impeachment trial of the Vice President.

“It wasn’t just the decision of the presiding officer. In fact, a lot of the presiding officer’s decisions were consulted with senator-judges,” Gatchalian said, adding that House prosecutors were free to present Trillanes voluntarily even without a subpoena.

Asked about Trillanes’ press conference last week alleging that Chinese funds flowed into a foundation and a company linked to the Vice President and her husband Manases Carpio, Gatchalian said the disclosures could guide senator-judges when the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), Bureau of Internal Revenue, banks and insurance firms testify this week on the unexplained wealth charge.
“What is important now is to validate whether the documents he has are the actual ones or not, whether they really came from the authorized government agencies,” Gatchalian said.

While noting that senator-judges have the leeway to ask the AMLC about Trillanes’ claims, Gatchalian said direct handlers of the financial records in question must be presented first to avoid hearsay.
He clarified that prosecutors can still call Trillanes to the witness stand afterwards.
No more Article III
House prosecutors confirmed anew that they would drop the bribery charges against Duterte during the resumption of trial this week.

“From our end and as we see it, we have been able to prove three articles already and we think that is enough, so at least trial will not continue into next year,” House prosecutor and Manila Rep. Joel Chua disclosed in a radio interview over the weekend.
“We are confident the three articles are enough to render justice to the Filipino people,” fellow prosecutor and Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong noted. – Delon Porcalla

articles.title: First Philippines ambassador to Bhutan presents credentials to king
articles.summary: The first Philippine ambassador to Bhutan presented his credentials to King Jigme Khesar Namgyel WangchuckWangchuck, officially embarking on his duties.

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — The first Philippine ambassador to Bhutan presented his credentials to King Jigme Khesar Namgyel WangchuckWangchuck, officially embarking on his duties.

Ambassador Josel Ignacio paid courtesy calls on senior Bhutanese officials in Thimphu on Sept. 18 as the Philippines’ first non-resident ambassador to the kingdom, hours after presenting his credentials to the king.

Ignacio was received in succession by officiating Prime Minister Lyonpo Lungten Dorji who is also minister for home affairs; and by Minister for foreign affairs and external trade Lyonpo D.N. Dhungyel, at the ministry’s headquarters, Gyalyong Tshokhang.

In both encounters, both sides welcomed the establishment of diplomatic relations between the Philippines and Bhutan less than a year before, on Oct. 6, and the accreditation in either country of their respective envoys.

Both Dorji and Dhungyel acknowledged the long-standing friendship and cooperative ties between the two countries, decades in advance of formal ties, especially the Philippines’ provision of technical training and education assistance to Bhutanese officials and students.
They expressed appreciation for the participation of Filipino volunteer trainers in Bhutan’s “De-Suung” (Guardians of Peace) Skilling Program for its youth.

articles.title: Warning aired on foreign-funded destabilization
articles.summary: Foreign-funded destabilization plots to undermine or overthrow a sitting administration are not far-fetched, according to a spokesperson for the prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice…

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 12:00am

Former Surigao del Norte congressman Robert Ace Barbers raised the possibility following former senator Antonio Trillanes IV’s allegations about nearly P500 million incash inflows to entities linked to Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Foreign-funded destabilization plots to undermine or overthrow a sitting administration are not far-fetched, according to a spokesperson for the prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

“This sounds like foreign-funded destabilization, if you put two and two together,” Barbers said. “I find ex-senator Trillanes’ revelations of China-sourced cash flows into local entities linked to VP Duterte and her spouse Manases Carpio disturbing.”

Trillanes, in a press conference on Oct. 2 at Club Filipino in San Juan, alleged that P319 million from the Chinese government and China-based corporations went to Cale88Foods Corp., a company linked to Duterte and her husband.
Another P150 million was purportedly funneled to the Tapang at Malasakit Foundation, which was also associated with Duterte. These transactions total P456 million.
The Vice President’s camp has dismissed Trillanes as a liar.

“We’re talking about nearly half a billion pesos here. What is this money for?” Barbers asked. “Is this payment in exchange for staying silent on the WPS (West Philippine Sea) issue, where the CCG (China Coast Guard) has made a habit of harassing Filipino fishermen in our own territory?”

“Or is this in exchange for a favor to undermine our own government before fellow Filipinos – from the executive, legislature and judiciary to our law enforcement authorities? To quote VP: I have no trust in the courts, I have no trust in the police,” he added.

Trillanes, an arch critic of the Duterte family, initially wanted to be a witness of the prosecution in the impeachment trial, but later decided to remove himself from the list, claiming “pressure” to keep him out of the trial.
He has declined to elaborate on the supposed pressure.
Barbers said Trillanes’ claims were consistent with the conduct of the Dutertes.

“If it is proven that China is taking advantage of our political situation to further their geopolitical and expansionist goals, shame on them. But what is even more shameful are Filipinos who allow themselves to be used by foreigners for money,” Barbers said.
Akbayan party-list also expressed similar concerns over the supposed funds from China.

“We are hearing allegations of hundreds of millions flowing from China into the networks of powerful politicians. While our fishermen and frontliners in the WPS are being harassed, it appears that some are profiting from their silence,” Akbayan stated.
“If proven, these allegations raise serious questions about corruption, accountability, national security and our sovereignty,” it declared.
The impeachment court is already set to hear Anti-Money Laundering Council testimony concerning inward remittances to Cale88 from China and other countries.
The prosecution is wrapping up the presentation of evidence on Article II, which covers allegations of unexplained wealth against Duterte.
