articles.title: Antigonish, N.S., sign condemned for depicting rape culture
articles.summary: A sign hung outside an off-campus house in Antigonish, N.S., during St. Francis Xavier University's homecoming weekend is being described as an example of rape culture and has drawn condemnation from…

image.caption: This sign was hung outside a house in Antigonish, N.S. (Tara Taylor)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

A sign hung outside an off-campus house in Antigonish, N.S., during St. Francis Xavier University's homecoming weekend is being described as an example of rape culture and has drawn condemnation from two universities and a professor who teaches at St. FX.
'I saw it as a taunt and just very much treating girlfriends as objects, as possessions,' says St. FX prof
The sign read "Drop-off zone: Acadia girlfriends."
Tara Taylor, a professor and the chair of the mathematics department at St. FX, saw the sign while driving home with her child on Friday evening. She returned later to take a photo of it.
"I thought I should really take a photo of it to document this," she said. "This is not OK and I don't want to contribute to the silence around it."
It's unclear why the sign targets Acadia students. There were no varsity games taking place on campus against the Wolfville, N.S., university Saturday.
St. FX has previously been criticized for how it handles sexualized violence on campus.

items: Former St. FX football player sentenced to 2 years in prison for sexual assaults
Complaints surface about recurring violence against women at St. FX
St. FX student accused of sexual assault withdraws, president apologizes

blocks.text: Taylor said there was another sign at the home that was more offensive, but she chose not to take a photo of it.
She posted the photo to Facebook to see if others had the same visceral reaction as she did. Taylor said people generally did.
"I saw it as a taunt and just very much treating girlfriends as objects, as possessions," she said. "I just found it very offensive and part of rape culture. I didn't see it as just a joke."
Taylor said the sign was removed by 11 a.m. AT on Saturday, but was back up later in the night. As of Sunday morning, it's unclear if the sign is still hanging.
St. FX statement

In a statement attributed to St. FX's vice-president of student life, Elizabeth Yeo, the university said it is investigating the matter and takes it very seriously. It said students found to violate the university's code of conduct will be held accountable.
"Conduct that demeans, objectifies or disrespects others has no place in the St. FX community," she wrote.
The statement called the sign offensive.
University's statement not strong enough, says Taylor
That wording bothers Taylor.
"I don't think it went far enough to condemn what it was," she said.

Taylor, who has taught at the university for 22 years, said not a year goes by when a student doesn't approach her to tell her they've been sexually assaulted, and she sees the consequences that has on them personally and academically.
"I would say women at St. FX have been kind of screaming about this for decades," she said.
Taylor said the school has made some changes over the years, including instituting a sexual violence policy and educating the community about consent.
But she said more could be done, including having men in leadership positions, coaches and team captains speak out and say situations like this are unacceptable.
St. FX issues second statement
On Sunday morning, St. FX issued a second statement, this one signed by president Andrew Hakin.
It called the sign degrading and deeply concerning.
"Language that objectifies women or makes light of sexualized violence has no place at St. FX or in any community," Hakin wrote.

"We understand the concern and anger this has caused, both within our own community and beyond it. St. FX unequivocally rejects misogyny, sexualized and gender-based violence, and the attitudes and behaviours that contribute to rape culture."
The statement said the university intervened to have the sign removed and when it was reposted, it took further action to have it taken down again. The university did not detail exactly what it did.
The statement said the matter has been referred to the university's discipline process.

"Every member of our community deserves to be treated with dignity and respect," Hakin wrote. "We all have a responsibility to challenge behaviour that diminishes others, normalizes sexualized violence, or undermines the safety and belonging of members of our community."
Acadia statement
Acadia also issued a statement and said the sign encouraged sexual violence against its students.

"What happened in Antigonish is a symptom of a society-wide problem," it said. "It is our collective responsibility as higher education institutions to speak out against violence against women, and rape culture specifically."
The university encouraged affected students to contact its sexualized violence response office for support.

articles.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.summary: Two residents in Mekelle tell the BBC pro-government forces have taken control of the city.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Sunday
ByTeklemariam Bekiteditor, BBC Tigrinya, and Jack Burgess
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.

Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.

Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.

blocks.caption: BBC map of Ethiopia showing the northern states of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. The regional capital of Mekelle is labelled in Tigray and the national capital Addis Ababa is also located near the centre of the country and just outside the three northern states. Eritrea is shown to the north, borderin…

blocks.text: On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.

Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.

The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: Debris found after medical plane carrying six people went missing off Nantucket
articles.summary:
Six passengers and crew on board still unaccounted for after medical transport plane vanishes over Atlantic, officials say

Researches found debris from a medical transport plane that was…

blocks.text: Researches found debris from a medical transport plane that was carrying six people when it vanished over the Atlantic early on Saturday during a flight from Bermuda to Boston, the US Coast Guard said.

A statement from the Coast Guard issued on Saturday evening said crews searching off the coast of the Massachusetts island Nantucket “located a debris field confirmed to be from the aircraft”, described as an air ambulance.

Six passengers and crew on board were still unaccounted for at the time of the debris field’s discovery, a spokesperson for the Coast Guard said. Boats, planes and helicopters were launched after flight controllers lost contact with the air ambulance.
Air traffic controllers had difficulty communicating with the flight in its final moments.
“You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12.46am. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?”
According to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, the pilot’s response was not audible.

The air ambulance – a Gulfstream G100 – took off from Bermuda late on Saturday, carrying a patient, a family member and a four-person crew. The patient and family member were identified as citizens of Bermuda. The crew was identified as Canadian citizens, though the names of the people on board the flight were not immediately released.

As it neared Nantucket, the plane reported electrical failures, according to radio transmissions. Data from the website FlightAware shows the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes and disappeared from radar shortly after at about 1am local time.
The Coast Guard said on Saturday evening that its William Sparling cutter boat would continue searching for those onboard the air ambulance through the night.
The agency reported that its crews searched roughtly 1,644 sq miles (4,258 sq km) for the aircraft in about 27 hours.
“Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night.”
Bermudian government officials said they had been in touch with the passengers’ families.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time,” Bermuda premier David Burt in a statement. “We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

articles.title: After a deadly paper mill explosion, a community in Washington state looks to a key House race
articles.summary:
In a district shaken by the deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seat

On a misty morning in May in south-west Washington state, Laura…

blocks.text: On a misty morning in May in south-west Washington state, Laura Oltmann, a 41-year-old dietitian, had barely clocked in when an unfamiliar overhead announcement echoed through the hospital.
“We get overhead pages for different types of emergencies. But this one, we don’t get very often,” recalled Oltmann.

Doctors, nurses and staff began guessing what could have happened. Perhaps it was a train derailment. Maybe a major highway crash. As the speculation grew, so did the uncertainty. Staff started calling one another. The answer shook them all. “Someone mentioned there had been an explosion at this plant, and that we were probably going to be getting some patients from there,” Oltmann said.

Forty miles south, in the port city of Longview, residents had awakened to a thunderous boom. At approximately 7.18am, as workers changed shifts at a paper mill company, Nippon Dynawave Packaging, a tank of white liquor, a caustic chemical used in the paper-making process, imploded. Hours passed with no explanation of what had caused it or how it could have happened at all, and suspicion began to brew.
With roughly a thousand people working at the mill, thousands more were waiting for a phone call. Parents called children. Wives called husbands. Grandparents called grandchildren.

blocks.caption: Damage at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging mill in Longview, Washington, after an implosion on 26 May. Photograph: Karen Ducey/The Seattle Times/AP

blocks.text: “For those that did not get that response,” said Jeff Wilson, a Republican state senator representing Longview, who also sits as the port commissioner, “all they got was silence.” In the end, 11 people were killed in one of Washington state’s deadliest industrial accidents in nearly a century.

Nowhere was that impact felt more deeply than in Longview itself, a working-class city of about 38,000 people whose economy and identity have long been tied to the paper industry, shipping and logging. For generations, families have depended on the mills for their livelihoods. The disaster struck at something the city had long regarded as permanent: the mills where generations had gone to work, and helped many send their children to college or put down a down payment on a home.

The implosion rippled through nearly every corner of a community affected by mill closures and economic change. Those concerns will likely have an impact at the ballot box. As summer turned toward fall and the leaves along the Columbia River began to turn yellow, memorial services gave way to campaign rallies. The same communities that had gathered around grieving families were preparing for one of the country’s most closely watched House races in November.

Nearly two months after the implosion, on 8 July, Wilson still spoke first about the workers, the funerals he had attended, the families and the co-workers who ran toward danger looking for one another. He recalled brothers Tyler and Brad Covington, 27 and 29; he said: “They went to work together. And then they died together.”

Before entering politics, Wilson spent more than 23 years cleaning tanks at the Nippon Dynawave mill. In the aftermath of the tragedy, he worked routinely with Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez’s office as local, state and federal officials responded to the disaster, his role in Olympia intersecting with hers in Washington.

blocks.caption: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez speaks to reporters. Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images

blocks.text: Though he declined to endorse her re-election, Wilson credited the Democratic congresswoman with being “present and accountable” and praised her for asking questions rather than “rubber-stamping anything”.

For a community divided by many of the same political forces pulling at the rest of the country, the disaster briefly created a sense of togetherness, as the whole community grieved the deaths of many of their neighbor and family members.

“Natural disasters will tend to bring people together,” said Mark Alan Smith, a political science professor at the University of Washington who studies American politics and religion. “It’s something people can unify around … across race and class and other divisions.”

On 4 August, Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican state senator John Braun advanced from a field of nine to face off for the district’s congressional seat in November. Braun finished first with about 39.7% of the vote to Gluesenkamp Perez’s 36.4%. Brent Hennrich, the progressive Democrat who argued that Gluesenkamp Perez no longer represented many of her party’s voters, took 16.7%.

The results exposed the competing pressures facing Gluesenkamp Perez heading into the general election. Braun finished ahead of the incumbent, while Hennrich’s showing demonstrated the size of the progressive bloc she will have to contend with in November. Many of those voters remain angry over parts of her vote on the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (Save) Act (which would require proof of citizenship to vote), ICE funding and a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity.

When asked about those direct criticisms of the congresswoman – whom many on the left feel has drifted from the party – her campaign responded with a written statement to the Guardian that cast her independence as the reason south-west Washington should return her to office. “DC has enough career politicians following national agendas,” said campaign manager Timothy Gowen. “Southwest Washington deserves an independent representative who delivers real results. Marie will always be loyal to her district first.” The statement did not address questions about her voting record or the primary result.

blocks.caption: John Braun at the capitol in Olympia last year. Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/AP

blocks.text: The race stretches far beyond Longview and the nearby city of Battle Ground. Washington’s third congressional district runs from the Pacific coast through the timber towns of the lower Columbia and inland farm country to Vancouver and the fast-growing suburbs north of Portland. Logging, paper mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life across much of it, while its politics pull hard in opposite directions.

That geography has forced Gluesenkamp Perez to build an unusual coalition. Her political survival has depended partly on voters who do not ordinarily identify with Democrats, including moderates and conservatives drawn to her emphasis on the trades, guns and independence from her party. But that same positioning has alienated Democrats who believe she has moved too far from them.

“Two years ago, people reported having to hold their nose and vote for her, because she was better than [former opponent and one-time counter-intelligence official] Joe Kent,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. “But now we’re in a situation where I’m hearing from so many people that even if she wins the primary, they will not vote for her. And the frustration is real. I’m feeling that personally.”

Thea Zaine, chair of the 20th Legislative District Democrats, speaks for the bloc of progressive Democrats whose discontent showed up in the primary returns. Her organization was the only Democratic party body in the district to endorse Hennrich.

“We believe in protecting immigrants. She’s voted to give more money to ICE,” Zaine said. “She voted to give funding to wars in Iran. And she takes money from Aipac, and she’s voted to fund the genocide in Gaza. She voted against the war powers resolution to rein in Trump.”
For Zaine, those votes have made the choice straightforward. But not every young, left-leaning voter who shares her frustration has reached the same conclusion.
Tanner Manley, 25, an incoming law student who lives near Vancouver and describes himself as left-leaning, shares much of the critique. He plans to vote for Gluesenkamp Perez anyway.

blocks.caption: Protesters gather in front of the Henry M Jackson federal building in Seattle. Photograph: Rio Giancarlo/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Of course, I wish more progressive candidates were viable here, and that Marie would take a clear moral stand on Israel and reject Aipac funding the way she refuses corporate Pac money,” he said. “In another race with different options, I’d likely support a different candidate.”

What keeps Manley with her is closer to home. After the Longview disaster, the US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, the independent federal agency investigating the tank failure at the Longview paper plant, faced elimination under the administration’s proposed budget. In June, Gluesenkamp Perez backed an amendment restoring $14m for the agency, which passed the House appropriations committee with Republican support.
“That might not satisfy progressives watching from the other side of the country,” Manley said, “but try telling people in this district that that kind of fight in Congress doesn’t matter.”

Neither candidate’s campaign has made the Longview tragedy a centerpiece of the race. A recent poll underscores how little room both candidates have: the survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided.
Smith, of the University of Washington, said events that bring communities together can be difficult to translate into partisan advantage.
“In order for something like that to affect how people vote, somebody has to channel it,” Smith said. “It’s hard to channel anything where everybody agrees.”

That could change, he said, “if you can somehow link your opponent to some negative aspect” of the event. So far, neither campaign has done so. And Wilson praised Gluesenkamp Perez’s handling of the disaster.
“She’s been representing, you know, from the federal angle, well on this,” he said.

The response also fit the political identity Gluesenkamp Perez has cultivated in south-west Washington, where she has emphasized the trades and the economic pressures facing rural and working-class communities. In an interview with OPB, she described watching the decline of industries that have long sustained towns across the region.
“Mill after mill close in our region,” she said. “It’s just got people really at high anxiety levels.”

A recent poll underscores how little room both House candidates have. The survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided.
About three miles north of Nippon Dynawave, at the Pentecostal church where Ron Peterson is pastor, the disaster remains part of the community’s memory.
For Peterson, 38, the tragedy had briefly brought together people who otherwise disagreed about much else. But when I asked him about politics, he drew a distinction.

blocks.caption: A vigil for the victims of the explosion. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters

blocks.text: “We don’t win politically,” he said. “We win spiritually.”

A few miles south, and across a district where the divisions are not only political, Chydell Armijo, 35, mother of two, was thinking about something more immediate. She had little enthusiasm for either political party. What worried her was whether people like her could still build a stable life: whether a small business could survive, whether her children could find opportunity and whether working people could still move up.
“I honestly feel like everybody is struggling,” Armijo said. “There is no such thing as middle class any more.”
For all the attention on which party will control this congressional seat after November, Armijo saw a divide that would remain regardless of who won.
“Our economic system has become difficult, in many ways, for us to climb,” she said.

articles.title: For advocates, CHED’s openness to lived names policy brings hope
articles.summary: There is no blanket policy yet that would allow transgender and queer students to be recognized by their lived names during graduation rites

blocks.text: PRIDE. Members of the LGBTQ+ community gather at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City for the annual Pride March, June 28, 2025.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
There is no blanket policy yet that would allow transgender and queer students to be recognized by their lived names during graduation rites

items: The Commission on Higher Education is open to discussing a policy that would allow transgender students to use their lived names during graduation ceremonies, which advocates view positively.
Advocates emphasize the need for comprehensive legislation, such as the SOGIESC bill, to promote inclusivity and address discrimination.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) has expressed openness to discussing a policy that would allow transgender and queer college students to use their lived names during graduation ceremonies, bringing hope to advocates.
Lived names are the chosen names of individuals used in daily life, different from their legal names.

“CHED actually does not see any legal impediment. CHED is, in fact, very open to a discussion regarding this,” Makati City 1st District Representative Monique Lagdameo said on September 23, during the plenary deliberations on the commission’s proposed 2027 budget in the House of Representatives.

Akbayan Representative Perci Cendaña brought the matter to the plenary after the Polytechnic University of the Philippines committed to allow its trans graduates to be recognized using their lived names during commencement exercises.

A similar policy was also implemented in other institutions such as the University of the Philippines, Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila, Philippine Normal University, De La Salle University, and Ateneo de Manila University, according to Cendaña.
However, Lagdameo, who spoke on behalf of CHED as its budget sponsor, noted that official records would still reflect the students’ names based on their birth certificates.

“I think maganda rin po itong way (this is a good way) for us to really navigate, how to literally open our minds and open our government into accepting and fully recognizing trans people and queer individuals with their lived name as well,” said Jira Samson, 22, who was not permitted to use her lived name during her graduation ceremony.
In an interview with Rappler, Samson, who recently graduated from Batangas State University, said the possible policy may benefit her “trans-siblings” who have just started their college journey.
Francheska Louise Chua, a 26-year-old medical student, said the openness to talks is a “big step forward” that could make a difference in the future.

But worries persist. “We are all scared, because as much as it is a conversation, hindi pa siya (it’s still not) undergoing implementation. So there’s still a big chance [a policy will not be issued],” she told Rappler.
“Obviously, there will be voters for yes or no, and it’s a long process…. This openness to conversations such as this is already a big step. So, as much as we are scared, we are still hopeful.”

Samson said university staff were sympathetic to her request to be recognized using her lived name during their graduation. But it was not granted as there was no specific CHED policy allowing for it to happen.
She noted that being recognized using one’s lived name is part of the gender-affirming and transitioning process of transgender and queer people, which must be respected.
Other than the recognition of lived names, Samson said dress code policies should be inclusive for LGBTQ+ students, and gender-responsive education must be strictly implemented.

“Ano ba naman po ‘yong i-recognize kami ng graduation, eh kung buong taon kami nakakaranas ng discrimination? Wala rin, ‘di ba?” she said. (What’s the use of being recognized by our lived name during graduation, if the whole year we experience discrimination? It would be useless, right?)
Recently, at Batangas State University, a transgender student was allegedly harassed by a security official as she was told to take off her bra in public because of dress code violations.

“It is just sad to note [that] such [a] university has not communicated this incident to CHED. But now that you have brought it to the attention of CHED, please know CHED will look into it and address the same,” Lagdameo told Cendaña during the September 23 budget deliberations.
CHED maintained it has existing memorandum orders recognizing the rights of students, as well as observing inclusivity in campuses.
Chua, who is a beauty queen, also conducts awareness campaigns about the LGBTQ+ community in Iloilo province.

But more than that, she believes the passage of a bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics (SOGIESC) “will really promote genuine inclusivity.”
In the 20th Congress, there are seven pending SOGIESC bills in the House, and two in the Senate.
The proposed measure has been languishing in Congress for over two decades already. (READ: Why is it taking so long to pass the SOGIESC bill?)

Ahead of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address in July, his son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, said he would be “happy to pass it when one comes to light,” but added that consultations are needed on whether or not it should be a priority bill.

blocks.caption: For advocates, CHED’s openness to lived names policy brings hope

blocks.text: Another pending proposal is the lived identities recognition bill, which seeks to allow transgender, intersex, and non-binary people to amend legal documents, specifically for name change and gender recognition, without going to court. – Rappler.com

articles.title: A swordfish was found on Haida Gwaii. Will more follow?
articles.summary: A University of British Columbia researcher says the finding is unusual but no longer unexpected due to warming waters worldwide, including in Canada.

image.caption: Quinn Barabash, or Captain Quinn as he is known in his videos, shared his discovery of a swordfish off B.C.'s North Coast across his YouTube and social media channels. (Quinn Barabash)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A University of British Columbia researcher says the finding is unusual but no longer unexpected due to warming waters worldwide, including in Canada.
UBC researcher says finding is unusual but no longer unexpected as Canadian waters warm
The discovery of a decaying swordfish off British Columbia's North Coast could be a sign of things to come as ocean temperatures rise, a researcher specializing in global fisheries says.
The fish was found by filmmaker and outdoorsman "Captain" Quinn Barabash while out with his oldest son and some friends on Sept. 27.
A video on his YouTube channel captures his incredulity when one of his shipmates tells him what they've found.
"That's crazy," he exclaims, moving towards the roughly six-foot-long (two-metre) carcass.

items: More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: Swordfish aren't unheard of in Canadian waters: recent years have seen Atlantic fisheries report historically high hauls of the animal.
But they are more commonly found in tropical and temperate waters, particularly in the Pacific.
Barabash's video was taken off the west coast of Haida Gwaii, where he lives, approximately 800 kilometres northwest of Vancouver.
In fact, he says he could only find two other documented sightings of swordfish in B.C., both far south and much closer to the Lower Mainland.
He rates seeing the swordfish in northwest B.C. as one of his wilder encounters.
"It's one of those things that kind of, I don't know, breaks the barriers in your mind of what is possible and achievable out there," he said.
"It's a wild open expanse, and once you go below the surface of the water, the mystery just increases."
Global trend

Isabella Morgante, a PhD student at the University of British Columbia's Institute for the Oceans and Fisheries, shared Barabash's wide-eyed enthusiasm for the find, confirming it as highly unusual and "really cool."
But once she got over her initial surprise, she also said it made sense that a fish normally found in more temperate waters may have made its way up north.
"It's become an increasingly common event along the B.C. coastline to see these tropical species coming up to colder waters to seek refuge from the warming oceans," the researcher said.
Through her work documenting the impacts of climate change on global fish patterns, she said there's a clear trend of people seeing sea creatures they aren't accustomed to.

A recent analysis, conducted in part by UBC researchers, found warming oceans were having an outsized impact in tropical regions — leading to lowered catches and unusual distribution of certain species.

items: Great white shark found dead on Haida Gwaii
Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns

blocks.text: Morgante also noted that it is an El Niño year, which means higher sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean.
But the researcher said the underlying trend shows the shifts in species distribution are more than just seasonal, but part of an ongoing shift that people out on the water should prepare for.
She said anyone who spots an unusual sea creature should do what Barbarash did: document it, take note of where it was found, and communicate the findings so researchers can record them.
And Barabash says he's going to keep on looking for new discoveries.
"The ocean is full of mysteries," he said.

articles.title: Teachers push P50k entry-level pay, higher allowances
articles.summary: A day before World Teachers" Day, teachers and education sector workers staged a protest outside the gates of Malacañang Palace on Sunday, calling for an entry-level salary of P50,000, higher…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 7:57pm

A day before World Teachers’ Day, teachers and education sector workers staged a protest outside the gates of Malacañang Palace on Sunday, calling for an entry-level salary of P50,000, higher allowances and a bigger national budget for education.

In a press release, the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) Philippines urged the Marcos administration to demonstrate its support for educators by increasing their pay and raising their Personnel Economic Relief Allowance (PERA) to P5,000 from the current P2,000.

Amid Congress’ deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget, the group also called for allocating 6% of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) to education to address persistent shortages, deteriorating school infrastructure and the worsening learning crisis.

"Matagal nang ipinagkikibit-balikat at dinadaan lang sa mga matatamis na papuri at pangako ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. ang tugon sa ating kagyat at makatwirang mga kahingian para sa disenteng sweldo, dagdag benepisyo, at sapat na pondo sa edukasyon,” ACT Secretary-General Raymond Basilio said.

(The Marcos Jr. administration has long brushed aside our urgent and reasonable demands for decent pay, higher benefits and adequate education funding, responding with nothing more than sweet praise and promises.)
Basilio said teachers, whom the administration has described as heroes and a top priority, tropped to the Palace gates to reiterate their demands to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

"Hamon namin sa Pangulo na patunayan ang kaniyang pagkilala hindi lamang sa mga talumpati at pahayag, kundi agarang iangat ang kalagayan ng mga guro, kawani at ng buong sektor ng edukasyon," he added.
(We challenge the President to prove his recognition not just through speeches and statements, but by immediately improving the welfare of teachers, staff and the entire education sector.)
The group also demanded accountability from the administration over alleged corruption and what it described as the continued underfunding of education and social services.
Tensions
Tensions flared during the protest as scuffles broke out between participating teachers and government security personnel.

In an update by Tuesday Niu of Super Radyo dzBB, security personnel from the Presidential Security Command were seen blocking and pushing back rallyists who attempted to stage a demonstration in front of a school inside the Malacañang Complex.
ACT Philippines strongly condemned what it described as the violent dispersal of protesters by police outside Malacañang.

In a report by Super Radyo dzBB reporter Luisito Santos, the group said 16 teachers and students were injured following the dispersal. It added that several belongings of the protesters were damaged and that authorities confiscated two megaphones.
To mark World Teachers’ Day on October 5, ACT Philippines announced that it would mobilize and march again toward Mendiola, joined by other government employees and civic groups.
The group's central call remains: “Dagdag sweldo, hindi dagdag trabaho! Ipaglaban ang karapatan at kagalingan, sapat na badyet at makabayang edukasyon!”
(Higher pay, not more workload! Fight for our rights and welfare, adequate funding and patriotic education!) — MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support
articles.summary:
Attack happened shortly after Merz arrived in city on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine

Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German…

blocks.text: Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.

A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.

The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

blocks.caption: Volodymyr Zelenskyy (left) and Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Bundesregierung/Tobias Koch/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.

Kyiv has come under near-constant attack from Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told Merz that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.
“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.

Russia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams.

blocks.caption: A Russian jet-powered drone strikes a bridge in Kyiv on 2 October. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: The attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter.
Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine.
“Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said.
A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.

In Moscow, some pro-war commentators noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator.

The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations.

Last month, Germany formally accused Moscow of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facing growing discontent at home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall.

Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made big electoral gains.

“Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis,” Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post.

articles.title: Torrential rain and flooding leave 2 dead and 1 missing in Spain's Catalonia region
articles.summary: Authorities warned of extreme danger around Barcelona and Girona, with rivers at risk of overflowing and residents urged to stay indoors.

image.caption: People watch the swollen Besos River after it exceeded its danger level following torrential rain near BarcelonaImage: Kike Rincón/Europa Press/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two people were reported dead on Sunday, with at least one person missing, after torrential rain triggered flooding in Spain's northeastern Catalonia region.
Authorities have warned of an "extreme danger" in parts of Barcelona and Girona, with rivers at risk of overflowing and residents in some areas urged to stay indoors.
What do we know about the victims?
One person died when a wall collapsed at a campsite in Tordera, north of Barcelona, while another drowned in a flooded garage in Montornes del Valles, Catalan firefighters said.
Emergency services were also searching for a missing person in Pineda de Mar, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) north of Barcelona.
Catalan regional leader Salvador Illa urged residents to exercise "the greatest caution" and follow instructions from emergency services.
How badly has Catalonia been hit?
More than 100 millimeters (3.9 inches) of rain fell overnight in numerous locations, according to Spain's AEMET weather agency.
Civil protection authorities sent alerts to people living near the Besos River warning of a risk of it bursting its banks. Residents were told to move to upper floors if flooding occurred.
Homes were flooded and vehicles submerged in towns near Barcelona, while local rail services were disrupted.
Emergency crews rescued people trapped in vehicles on flooded streets in Granollers and other communities.
Heavy storms in eastern Spain cause major floods
Flights at Barcelona airport were also canceled or delayed, while shops closed early and sporting and cultural events were called off.
What is causing the extreme weather?
The storms are linked to a weather phenomenon known in Spain as a DANA, traditionally called a "gota fria," or "cold drop."
It occurs when cold air high in the atmosphere meets warm, moisture-laden air rising from the Mediterranean, producing intense thunderstorms.
Spain's geography can amplify the effect, as moist air from the Mediterranean is forced upwards by mountain ranges separating the coast from the country's elevated interior.
The latest flooding comes almost two years after catastrophic floods linked to a DANA killed 238 people in eastern Spain, mostly in Valencia, in October 2024.
A study published in 2026 found that human-caused climate change intensified the rainfall during that disaster.
The findings apply only to the 2024 Valencia floods, and a separate analysis would be needed to determine the influence of climate change on the latest flooding in Catalonia.

articles.title: ‘Forgotten Island’: Filipino American stories are Filipino stories
articles.summary: 'Forgotten Island' is definitely an achievement worth celebrating, but Filipino storytelling does not begin nor does it end here. We have to take it upon ourselves to add to the narrative and tell…

blocks.text: October is Filipino American History Month.

And when award season rolls around in early 2027, I hope Filipinos back home, Filipino Americans, and others all around the world will be cheering for DreamWorks Animation’s Forgotten Island. It was a feat — and feast — for the senses. It was a fast-paced film, packed with ’90s nostalgia, provincial life, and filled to the brim with food, cultural nuance, music, and karaoke singing.

It captured everything that makes us Filipino: from our hospitality, love of family, and respect for elders to the underlying tension that comes with all that is deeply ingrained in the Filipino story.

As a Filipino American who lived in the Philippines for 10 years as a journalist — learning to speak Tagalog and improving my Cebuano to near fluency — I also noticed the Americanisms of the film, but I was not bothered by them, unlike some criticism I saw on social media. In my opinion, it did not diminish the Filipino-ness of the work.

When I used to go on Twitter, I would often see the “Filipino vs. Fil-Am” discourse, which inevitably surfaced again when this film came out, although to a lesser extent than I had seen in previous years.

But to me, nitpicking a character’s accent, scrutinizing the authenticity of folklore, or quibbling over “tayo na” vs. “tara na” misses the point entirely. (Both terms are accurate anyway, and anyone who thinks “tayo na” is wrong just needs to listen to more OPM.)
Because folklore isn’t even the most relatable part of the film to Filipinos.

The film’s true resonance lies in the parts of the story that take place outside of the mythical island of Nakali. It is Jo’s dad calling to say he isn’t taking her to America — a painful reality for millions of Filipino children left behind by migrating parents. And it is a story I sought to highlight when I was Rappler’s overseas Filipinos editor over a decade ago.
It is the immense pressure Raissa faces from her family to leave the Philippines because success so often dictates leaving home behind.
It is the overwhelming grief of leaving behind your friends and community once you board that flight, knowing that the move is likely for good.

An American colleague of mine was shocked to learn that the Philippines has entire government institutions built specifically to address overseas Filipino issues, driven by the country’s reliance on overseas remittances. Whether it intended to or not, this film may have been a first window, or conversation starter, for millions of non-Filipinos, who may not have realized there are countries like the Philippines where not being able to see your children grow up is just…life.

For me, the Filipino story here is not just one of creatures, spirits, magic. It is one of leaving, and returning — we even have a word for that: “balikbayan.” And, once you do leave, it is about never forgetting where you came from, navigating a new world that expects you to change, but never being able to fully leave behind the place and the people you came from. So you always return.
I won’t dig into the deep-seated disconnects between Filipinos in the motherland and those in the diaspora. Instead, I choose to focus on what binds us.

I don’t see the story of Filipinos in the Philippines and the story those abroad as two separate stories — they are one. A Filipino is a Filipino wherever they are — whether or not they speak fluent Filipino, and whether the last time they stepped foot home was a year ago, a decade ago, or 40 years ago. The through line of our collective story emanates from the cities and provinces, stretches out across oceans to the diaspora, and, for many born overseas like me, finds its way back again.

I understand the frustration or disappointment of viewers who may not see their exact representation as a Filipino in a single movie. But, for me, the amazing thing about living today is that we don’t have to put all our hopes for representation in one piece of work. Nor do we need Hollywood to tell or to validate our story.

While it is exciting to see our stories distributed to a massive global audience — and I will be loudly cheering for this film to win an Oscar — hopefully with all the other Filipinos. Respectfully, seeking validation from Hollywood is tired and overrated.

Yes, Forgotten Island is definitely an achievement worth celebrating, but Filipino storytelling does not begin nor does it end here.If you want true representation, I say we have to take it upon ourselves to add to the narrative and tell the story of the Filipino as we know it. Write it. Speak it. Sing it. Paint it. Draw it. Tell it however you can — with whatever platforms you have. Neither Hollywood, nor any other big machine in the west, is the validator of our experiences as Filipinos. We are. – Rappler.com
Ryan Macasero is a reporter for the Mercury News, covering the city of San Jose, California. He is a former Rappler multimedia reporter and editor of the #BalikBayan section.

articles.title: Japan: US Marine arrested in Okinawa on suspicion of murder
articles.summary: The Japanese government has lodged an official protest with Washington after a US Marine was arrested on suspicion of murdering a woman in Okinawa — where incidents involving US service personnel are…

image.caption: The US Marine Corps confirmed that a serviceman based at Marine Corps Air Station at Futenma, Okinawa, was in Japanese custodyImage: Chermaine Lee/DW

blocks.text: A United States Marine was arrested on suspicion of murder in Okinawa, Japan, police said Sunday, prompting an official protest from the Japanese government.
The 20-year-old lance corporal is suspected of robbing and murdering a 39-year-old woman in a hotel in Naha, the capital of Japan's most southernmost prefecture.
Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported that CCTV footage showed a foreign man entering a hotel room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and who voluntarily accompanied them to a local police station where he was arrested.
The suspect reportedly denies the charges.
What have Japanese officials said?

"The occurrence of ​such an extremely brutal and vicious incident is extremely regrettable," said Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ​in a statement as Tokyo registered an official protest with Washington.

blocks.caption: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has lodged an official complaint with WashingtonImage: Yudai Kato/Jiji Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The government of Japan strongly protests to the US side and strongly seeks maximum cooperation with the investigation," she continued, also calling for "stricter discipline among US military personnel" and "thorough measures" to prevent a recurrence.

According to the local Asahi Shimbum newspaper, the brother of the victim said: "We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened. My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter."
The US Marine Corps confirmed that a serviceman assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station at Futenma, Okinawa, was in Japanese custody.
"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the ⁠highest ​standards of behavior," it said in a statement.

The US Ambassador to Japan, George Glass, said he had spoken with Japan's Foreign Ministry and Okinawa's governor, offering "sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues."
Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why
How many US Marines are in Okinawa — and why?
The United States has around 54,000 military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, stationed in Japan. Most are based in Okinawa, which the US captured during the Second World War and held until 1972.
Located only 100 kilometers (60 miles) from Taiwan at the closest point, Okinawa is considered by both Tokyo and Washington to be key in deterring potential aggression from China in the region.

But the US presence regularly stirs resentment among local residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel, with crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run incidents and drunk-driving accidents.
"Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen," said Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, around 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Okinawa since 1972. In 2024, that number hit 80, the highest in 20 years.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine to seven years in prison after finding him guilty of choking and attempting to rape a young woman.
In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.

articles.title: Carlos Yulo to get P4 million for golden double as medalists cash in on Asian Games success
articles.summary: Gymnastics star Carlos Yulo once again reaps the financial rewards of his brilliance after winning two of the Philippines' four gold medals in the 2026 Asian Games

blocks.text: ALL HEART. Gold medalist Carlos Edriel Yulo of the Philippines celebrates after winning the men's vault final in the 2026 Asian Games.
Edgar Su/REUTERS
Gymnastics star Carlos Yulo once again reaps the financial rewards of his brilliance after winning two of the Philippines' four gold medals in the 2026 Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – Two years after receiving more than P100 million in incentives and rewards for his Olympic exploits, Carlos Yulo will benefit from another cash windfall after leading the Philippines’ campaign in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

The artistic gymnastics star will get P4 million from the government following his golden runs in the men’s floor exercise and vault — the same events in which he won his two Olympic gold medals at the 2024 Paris Games.

Under Republic Act No. 10699 or the National Athletes and Coaches Benefits and Incentives Act, Yulo is entitled to P2 million for each of his two gold medals. Meanwhile, silver and bronze medalists stand to receive P1 million and P400,000, respectively.
Yulo joined an exclusive list of Filipino athletes who won multiple golds in a single Asian Games edition, becoming only the eighth member of the club.

Others who achieved the feat were swimmers Artemio Salamat (two in 1951), Jacinto Cayco (two in 1951), and Haydee Coloso (two in 1954), tennis player Raymundo Deyro (two in 1958), athletics icon Mona Sulaiman (three in 1962), bowling legend Bong Co (three in 1978 and two in 1986), and golfer Yuka Saso (two in 2018).
In ruling the Asian Games, Yulo completed his collection that also includes titles from the World Championships, Asian Championships, World Cup, and Southeast Asian Games.
Pole vaulter EJ Obiena and taekwondo jin Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape will receive P2 million each after delivering the Philippines’ two other gold medals.

Obiena stands to pocket more after breaking his own Asian Games mark by clearing 5.91 meters. Under RA 10699, athletes who surpass a Philippine record or any ranking in a measurable international sports competition are entitled to additional cash incentives, with the amount to be determined by the Philippine Sports Commission.
The only Asian to clear six meters, Obiena became only the fourth back-to-back men’s pole vault champion in the history of the continental showpiece.

Meanwhile, Yape will bag an additional P400,000 after also winning bronze in the men’s individual poomsae before striking gold in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo, an event that debuted at the Asian Games.
The victory made Yape the first-ever Filipino to capture a taekwondo gold in the quadrennial meet.

Aside from the four golds, the Philippines claimed nine silvers and 16 bronzes for a total of 29 medals — its most in six decades — as it replicated its 17th-place finish in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China.

The incentives may ease the disappointment for athletes who fell short of gold as mixed martial artist Jean Claude Saclag, archer Amaya Amparo Cojuangco, taekwondo jins Juliana Mykhail Candelaria, Tachiana Mangin, and Kurt Barbosa, boxer Carlo Paalam, and jiu-jitsu athlete Alexandria Enriquez will earn P1 million each for their silvers.

In team events, the silver medalists in women’s 3×3 basketball — Kacey dela Rosa, Kennan Ka, Amyah Espanol, and Maria Pasilang — and women’s sepak takraw double — Jean Marie Sucalit, Abegail Sinogbuhan, and Nelly Jay Salon — will share the incentives provided under the law.
Teams with less than five members will equally split the rewards, while those part of squads with five or more participants will receive 25% of the incentives given to individual medal winners.
So Dela Rosa, Ka, Espanol, and Pasilang will get P250,000 each, while Sucalit, Sinogbuhan, and Salon will pocket P333,300.33 each.
Another big winner is weightlifter Albert Ian delos Santos, who will cash in more than P400,000 for his bronze after establishing new world junior and Asian junior records in the men’s 70kg class.

articles.title: 'This is not reconciliation,' judge says, scolding Canada for dragging feet on First Nations land debt deal
articles.summary: A federal judge recently said the way Canada has continued to "shirk its responsibilities" to a group of Manitoba First Nations since signing a landmark agreement meant to resolve historic treaty…

image.caption: The Manitoba Framework Agreement was signed in 1997 by the federal government, the provincial government and the Treaty Land Entitlement Committee of Manitoba, to give land to eligible First Nations. (CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A federal judge recently said the way Canada has continued to "shirk its responsibilities" to a group of Manitoba First Nations since signing a landmark agreement meant to resolve historic treaty land shortages "is simply not acceptable."
'Disheartening' to see 'more broken promises' under landmark 1997 Manitoba agreement: Justice Julie Blackhawk

The province, the federal government and the Treaty Land Entitlement Committee of Manitoba signed the Manitoba Framework Agreement in 1997 to give land to First Nations that were given insufficient land under Treaties 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10.

The total land owed to the 21 First Nations eligible under the agreement is about 445,000 hectares. Just over half of that has been converted to reserve land as of last March, the committee's annual report said.
In an Aug. 21 decision, Federal Court of Canada Justice Julie Blackhawk expressed frustration with Ottawa's ongoing delays in fulfilling its commitments under the deal.

"It is disheartening to see that three decades after the successful negotiation of a modern agreement aimed at settling outstanding Treaty obligations, the relationship between the parties continues to be marred by distrust and now represent[s] more broken promises," she wrote.
"It is difficult for this court to see how the Crown is committed to reconciliation in the face of the Crown's conduct on this matter."

Ottawa has delayed implementation of the 1997 agreement with "vague references" about its duty to consult other Indigenous communities, but Blackhawk said that duty "does not detract" from Canada's obligation to fulfil its obligations under the deal.

"Canada cannot hide behind a vaguely defined duty to consult to hold up its fulfillment of the settlement for an indefinite period of time," she wrote. "This is not reconciliation [or] upholding the honour of the Crown."

items: Manitoba First Nations seek to sue Canada for not honouring treaty land entitlements

blocks.text: While the federal government told Blackhawk it is committed to advancing reconciliation, the judge said that promise "rings hollow in the circumstances of this case."
Blackhawk's ruling was the result of a summary judgment motion by the committee as part of its 2022 statement of claim against Ottawa over breaches of the 1997 deal.

The lawsuit's roots go back a decade. In 2016, the Treaty Land Entitlement Committee used the deal's dispute resolution process to allege Canada's consultation with the Métis — before setting aside lands under the 1997 agreement — failed to comply with the deal, Blackhawk said.
In 2018, an independent arbitrator found Canada materially breached the agreement's fundamental terms requiring it to use "best efforts" and refrain from unilateral changes to the deal, she wrote.

Canada did not remedy those breaches, and in 2021, the federal court ruled the First Nations were no longer bound by terms of individual treaty land entitlement agreements preventing them from pursuing legal action against the government for insufficient land allocations under the treaties, Blackhawk wrote.
'We need the land': committee president

The federal government said it respects Blackhawk's decision and is reviewing it but will not comment further while the committee's lawsuit is before the courts, spokesperson Pascal Laplante told CBC News in a written statement.
Although Blackhawk handed down criticism of Canada's conduct, her ruling came with mixed results for both sides.
She dismissed the federal government's argument that the Treaty Land Entitlement Committee must first exhaust the agreement's dispute resolution process to pursue relief for its breaches of the deal.

But Blackhawk sided with Ottawa's argument that the 1997 agreement and the treaty land entitlements operate prospectively, rejecting the committee's claim that the amount of land owed under the deal was retroactive to the initial signing of the treaties.

items: Manitoba First Nations say fulfil promise and turn over more treaty land

blocks.text: She also ruled in favour of Canada's argument that the total amount of land owed to each First Nation in the 1997 agreement and individual treaty land entitlements were negotiated amounts "based on mutual compromises" and did not reflect actual reserve land entitlements under the treaties.

Seeking an out-of-court resolution, negotiators previously reached a proposed settlement in 2023, which included a $3.5-billion compensation package for the loss-of-use of reserve lands, but it "evaporated," the Treaty Land Entitlement Committee said in a news release earlier this year.

Committee president Nelson Genaille said in a June 2026 letter to federal Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty that the proposed settlement was "designed to avoid expensive and prolonged years of litigation."

The proposed settlement also included amendments to the 1997 agreement that would have remedied Canada's breaches of the deal and introduced a process for the federal government to consult other Indigenous groups, wrote Genaille, who's also chief of Sapotaweyak Cree Nation.

In 2025, Alty's predecessor Gary Anandasangaree announced a $210-million payment to the affected First Nations in advance of the proposed settlement, the Treaty Land Entitlement Committee's news release said.
Genaille told CBC News the committee plans to appeal Blackhawk's ruling.
Canada needs to fulfil its obligations to the First Nations under the 1997 deal, he said.
"Basically, they want to keep us in the teepees, when the treaties were signed," Genaille said Friday.
"We know how to do business. We want to be part of the economy, and in order for us to be part of the economy, we need the land that's been obligated to us ... so we could start those businesses."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ozten Shebahkeget is a member of Northwest Angle 33 First Nation, born and raised in Winnipeg. She started writing for CBC Manitoba during the first Pathways program in 2022. She holds a master's degree in writing from the University of Saskatchewan.

articles.title: Jacob Rees-Mogg accuses Tucker Carlson of ‘verging on defending Hitler’
articles.summary:
Former Tory minister defends UK decision to enter war in podcast with US rightwinger and Putin sympathiser

The former Tory minister Jacob Rees-Mogg has found himself defending Britain’s…

blocks.text: The former Tory minister Jacob Rees-Mogg has found himself defending Britain’s decision to fight against Adolf Hitler after inviting the US rightwinger and Vladimir Putin sympathiser Tucker Carlson into his home for an interview.
During the encounter, Carlson repeatedly suggested the west was to blame for inviting aggression from Russia and said of the prospect that Britain could have lost to Hitler: “Who cares?”
Rees-Mogg, who lost his parliamentary seat in 2024, appears to have agreed to host Carlson’s podcast show after carving out a post-politics career as a commentator.

Carlson set up the show after leaving Fox News and losing faith with Donald Trump, largely citing the US president’s willingness to get involved in foreign wars. Carlson has interviewed Putin and taken a sympathetic position towards Russia over Ukraine.
In the lengthy debate on foreign policy and global tensjons, the US commentator repeatedly goaded Rees-Mogg over the smallness of the UK armed forces and suggested Russia was more powerful.
Rees-Mogg explained that the UK economy was bigger and made the case that Britain and western allies had to support Ukraine and deter Russian aggression.
Carlson went on to question why Britain bothered entering the second world war and claimed Germany had a legitimate claim over parts of Poland.
Rees-Mogg said: “Otherwise we’ll be speaking German.”
Carlson replied: “Who cares? There are a lot of people in Britain who can’t speak English. So it would be nice to have at least a European language spoken in your country.”
During the interview, Rees-Mogg said he was very surprised that Carlson was “verging on defending Hitler”, adding: “I think this is not really what you want to be doing.”
Carlson replied: “Yeah, I guess I’m just a secret Nazi. I’m actually not a secret Nazi … and hardly a public Nazi.”
Rees-Mogg responded that he was reassured, before saying that “Germany would have invaded us” if the UK had not gone to war.

The interview has raised eyebrows in the US as well as Britain, with Mike Huckabee, the Republican and US ambassador to Israel, posting on X: “When it seemed impossible for Toxic Tucker to descend deeper into the sewer here he goes opining that UK should have let Nazis take over. Forget that Hitler murdered 11 million people? I thought Tucker was against killing? He needs help. Serious help.”

articles.title: Chinese Embassy rejects 'smear campaign' over teacher exodus
articles.summary: The Chinese Embassy in Manila on Sunday rejected what it called “malicious smear campaigns” claiming that Chinese-language teachers in the Philippines were returning to China due to safety concerns.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 6:44pm
The Chinese Embassy in Manila on Sunday rejected what it called “malicious smear campaigns” claiming that Chinese-language teachers in the Philippines were returning to China due to safety concerns.

In an online statement, Chinese Embassy spokesperson Ji Lingpeng addressed queries about alleged attacks on educational exchanges and reports that Chinese-language teachers were leaving the country because of a hostile environment.

“We firmly reject the baseless accusations and strongly denounce the malicious smear campaigns targeting educational and people-to-people exchanges between China and the Philippines, including Chinese-language education in the Philippines,” Ji said.
The embassy called on the Philippines to ensure that the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese nationals in the country are protected.

Ji said cultural and educational exchanges between the two countries had played an important role in fostering mutual understanding, adding that Chinese-language teachers had helped promote Chinese culture in the Philippines.

“We believe those malicious rhetoric and actions against China-Philippines people-to-people exchanges by certain individuals have no place in the Philippines, and the time-honored friendship between the Chinese and Filipino peoples will continue to stand,” Ji said.
The statement came amid criticism of Chinese-language education programs from retired US Air Force Colonel Ray Powell of the SeaLight project and Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.— MCG, GMA News
