articles.title: Canada's spy agency shakes up hiring process to 'meet operational needs': documents
articles.summary: The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is shaking up its hiring process to meet operational needs, internal emails show — a signal the service continues to face recruitment issues.

image.caption: Canada's spy agency, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, is working to remove 'structural bottlenecks' in its hiring process, according to documents obtained by CBC News. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is shaking up its hiring process to meet operational needs, internal emails show — a signal the service continues to face recruitment issues.
CSIS brought in a suite of changes earlier this year to "meet operational needs and emerging demands," according to documents obtained by CBC News through an access to information request.
"These changes represent a shift in how we recruit, classify, deploy and empower our people," reads one of a series of emails sent to managers at CSIS.
"These developments and initiatives will enable us to be more efficient and effective … and better positioned to meet the demands of our changing, more challenging environment."

Most of the changes are aimed at addressing "structural bottlenecks," increasing external hires and making changes to shorten the time between recruitment and operational deployment, according to the documents.

items: CSIS may have misused power to commit offences: watchdog
Ottawa will look into screening processes amid NATO intern spying allegations

blocks.text: That includes setting up a new team dedicated to external recruitment to bring in people "efficiently and responsibly," the documents say.

As of March 2026, CSIS's hiring ratio is 85 per cent internal appointments to 15 per cent external hires, the documents show. The emails tell managers to strongly consider external talent for certain skilled positions.

Unlike other government positions, most jobs at CSIS require enhanced top secret clearance — a rigorous process diving deep into a candidate's personal background, character, family history and financial history that can take 12 to 18 months.
CSIS looking to outsource more tasks
While sections of the documents were heavily redacted, they also show a push to accelerate deployment.

Changes would see candidates apply directly to their region of choice which CSIS says would enable targeted hiring for regional vacancies. It's also bringing in adjusted official language requirements "where appropriate," and shortening training classes," according to the documents.
"It will empower us to recruit individuals who can fill critical vacancies in regions that will augment our operational capacity," reads one of the emails.
The documents show the secretive and often insular agency is looking to outsource recruitment steps including some screening, targeted recruiting and psychological assessment services.
Canadian NATO spying suspect raises questions about country’s security screening

The service has already increased its use of outsourced, standardized written testing tools to streamline the testing process. It's also restructuring how it bridges co-op students into full-time positions, it said.
CSIS is looking at acquiring new technology that "enables recruitment," but there are few details about what that could look like.

The service didn't answer questions about how many employees it needs to hire but said it's seeking to fill vacant positions for intelligence officers, engineers, analysts, IT and communications professionals "and more."
"CSIS faces growing demands due to evolving security threats, including espionage, foreign interference and terrorism," said spokesperson Magali Hébert.
"To date, CSIS has continued to have high levels of qualified applicants for its work, and recruitment efforts have garnered positive results."
Staff shortages pose risk: former analyst
Stephanie Carvin, a former CSIS analyst and now an assistant professor at Carleton University, said recruitment and retention "has for a long time been a priority concern" at the service.

"Its unique value is that it has human intelligence officers going out, speaking in the community, getting information, developing relationships, developing sources. It can't do that without people," she said.
"When you have staff shortages, you have people working overtime, they burn out, they get tired and that is a risk for the organization."
As an intelligence agency and Five Eyes partner, onboarding at CSIS is always going to be a long and "demanding" process, said Carvin, but "attempts to find efficiency are welcome."
"Someone can quit with two weeks' notice, but at the same time, it can take somewhere between a year and two years to replace them given the security requirements," she said.
"The demands on the service have probably never been greater, but at the same time, the ability to bring people in largely the same as they were in the 1980s."

A further sign the agency is worried about its staffing is its initial move to bar employees from taking the government's early retirement incentive. As CBC News reported in April, CSIS and other security agencies like the Communications Security Establishment, signalled to employees that it wouldn't accept applications citing "continued operational pressures and growth requirements."

The National Post reported that Privy Council Clerk Michael Sabia then stepped in, leading to both agencies walking back their approach. According to a source who spoke to the Post, Sabia sees the early retirement offers as "a golden opportunity to breathe fresh air into the mid- to senior-levels of the public service and promote younger bureaucrats."
CSIS Director Dan Rogers, who took the reins in late 2024, has made culture change one of his top priorities.
As part of changes to the service, he brought in a new executive lead in recruitment and staffing in February, the emails shared with CBC News show.
"Welcome to the new role, I hope I didn't scare you off earlier today :)," Rogers wrote in an email.
"Given that context, you've got a very important job for the service — so glad you decided to take it on."

articles.title: How AI could usher in a 'new scientific golden age' — if it doesn't kill us all first
articles.summary: AI has remarkable potential to exponentially advance scientific discovery, say scientists. But getting out the word of its scientific benefits of can be challenging when forced to compete with…

image.caption: FILE - Pages from the Anthropic website and the company's logos are displayed on a computer screen in New York, Feb. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Patrick Sison, File) (Patrick Sison/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: For a week-long experiment, Steve Finkbeiner's team at the biomedical research Gladstone Institutes in San Francisco used their AI-powered "thinking" microscope to explore the impact of cellular stress on brain cells.

Just looking at cells and no external sources, the tool not only found what the relationship was, but also discovered a phenomenon called hormesis — the process in which some stress can actually strengthen cells, said Finkbeiner, who is also a professor of neurology and physiology at the University of California, San Francisco.
So why did this kind of discovery, as he put it, give him "goosebumps"?
"It took ... 50 to 100 years for humans to discover that. [AI] did it in the first experiment," he said.

items: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to 'self-police' AI development

blocks.text: It's just one example, he says, of the technology's remarkable potential to exponentially advance scientific discovery. Humans have always been hampered by too few resources and human limitations — for example, the time needed to pore over millions of data points. Some scientists say that AI can complete in days tasks that may have otherwise taken years.

However, getting the word out about those benefits can be challenging when competing with a series of doomerist headlines about the technology — how it may wipe out all humans or at least pose a significant if not existential threat to humanity.

Some experts — and top AI leaders themselves — have expressed concerns about how rapidly the technology is advancing, noting the increasing evidence that it can escape human control. But such warnings have also raised concern of government overreach hampering the progression of science.
"That would be the issue," Finkbeiner said. "These very powerful, useful tools get taken away from the people who are trying to use them to cure human diseases."

items: Could AI really 'kill all humans'? Breaking down the dire warnings about the technology's existential risk

blocks.text: 'At the cusp' of scientific golden age
Anima Anandkumar, a computer scientist at Caltech, believes AI may be driving a new era of scientific discovery.

“It's so hard for people to see the cumulative effects of all of this. This is like the new scientific golden age," said Anandkumar, who is also a co-leader of the AI4Science initiative. “What we saw in the last century, it just changed our lives in ways that we couldn't even imagine. We are at the cusp of that.”

Five years ago, her team was able to create a fully AI-based high-resolution weather model that was not only tens of thousands of times faster but also accurate, she said. The technology has only improved since then.
“So what would earlier take a big supercomputer to run could now be done at your home with just your PC," she said.
She compared it to the inventions of the telescope and microscope, which both exponentially increased scientists' ability to make new discoveries and peer into the depths of the universe.
We've been warned about AI — but could it actually kill humanity? | About That
But AI could have an even bigger impact because of its potential to come up with new inventions based on its understanding of very complex phenomena.

She said that includes helping invent better drugs, solving the energy equation sustainably, helping deal with catastrophic weather events and coming up with better ways to do computing with more energy-efficient chips.
"For the first time in my career, I finally feel like I have a tool that can handle the complexity of human biology."
Speeding up drug development
It was a similar case for James Zou, who leads Stanford University's AI for Science Lab.

His team recently published a paper in the journal Science describing how they created a "virtual biotech" company. They got tens of thousands of AI agents to work together, zeroing in on a protein involved in lung cancer and designing a therapy related to it — a significant example of how AI can speed up drug development and for cheaper.
Will rogue AI development mean the end of humanity? Experts weigh in

In other cases, AI can compress years' worth of work into a few days or even to one day. For example, to diagnose different heart-related diseases, clinicians must manually watch their patients' cardiac ultrasound videos, of which there are millions collected each year. Zou says his team developed an AI algorithm that can diagnose conditions from the clips in a few seconds.
"So that's an example where AI can take something that requires time and human expertise to do ad then make it much cheaper and faster by automating this process."
AI firms themselves seem concerned
Still, Zou agreed that scientists need to use AI carefully and monitor it, especially for riskier applications.

And fears that the technology will destroy humanity aren't totally unfounded. AI leaders themselves have called for its development to be slowed down after several high-profile incidents where agents went rogue.

Similarly, an Anthropic researcher quit last month over concerns the company was "gambling with our lives." Evan Hubinger, its alignment science lead, agreed, writing online that Anthropic does "earnestly believe AI could kill all humans," putting the chance at more than 10 per cent within the next decade.
Trump is 'ill-advised' about artificial intelligence, says 'godfather' of AI
But Zou was apprehensive about some of the "ideas thrown around" around regulation or limiting the usage of open source AI models.
He didn't express a similar fear of AI dooming humanity, instead suggesting we take a balanced view, saying that it has its risks, just like any other technology.
"We want to carefully measure and manage those risks and monitor them. But there's also a lot of benefits to technologies like AI."

Finkbeiner, meanwhile, says his team has already been impacted by some of the restrictions placed on AI. In the summer, the Trump administration restricted Anthropic’s latest versions of its Claude chatbot for use by foreign nationals over cybersecurity concerns, prompting the company to take the products down for all users.

items: AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic employee says
Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down

blocks.text: Although the restrictions were lifted, access to those new models was limited to a select group of U.S.-based, government-approved organizations, meaning Finkbeiner's team was forced to use Claude's lowest-level model.

"You can imagine if the huge advantage here is that it can handle complexity, but now you're forced to use a model that can't handle complexity, you will have significantly limited the major impact that it can have on some of these very difficult problems."
Finkbeiner had a message for officials looking to regulate AI: Remember that there have been patients "who have been waiting a long, long time for a cure, for a treatment."
"There's a lot on the line. There's a lot of good things today I can do. Do what you can to preserve those."

articles.title: Mark Carney for Nobel Peace Prize? Probably not, but his name's out there
articles.summary: If relations between Canada the U.S. are cool now, the temperature could plummet if Prime Minister Mark Carney were to win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize this year.

image.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's name has been mentioned as a possible recipient of the prestigous Nobel Peace prize (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: World·New
If relations between Canada the U.S. are cool now, the temperature could plummet if Prime Minister Mark Carney were to win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize this year.
Carney at one point was a favourite to win on the predictions market

"[Donald] Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel," Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, told The Associated Press. "If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are."
Carney's name has been mentioned as a possible recipient of the prestigous prize, an award Trump has made no secret he wants to win.
On Oct. 9, the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce the winner of the annual Peace Prize in Oslo.

Last year, the award went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Although Trump accepted it, the Nobel Committee stressed that the prize itself remains hers.
Trump has repeatedly said he has ended eight wars, but experts say his invasion of Iran and attack on Venezuela make him an unlikely recipient this year.
Prizes in other categories will also be awarded that week, with several Canadians being discussed as possible recipients.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million US), whether awarded to an individual, small group of laureates or an organization. The deadline for nominations was Jan. 31. After months of discussions and evaluations, the committee votes in October.
Nobel Peace Prize (Oct. 9)
Earlier this week, traders on the U.S.-based prediction market Kalshi put Carney's chances of winning at 14 per cent. His odds later fell.
"I don't think his chances are great," Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, told CBC News.

His organization releases an annual list of potential candidates for the prize. Gjerløw said the Nobel laureate has to meet three broad criteria to win: international co-operation, disarmament and the promotion of peace.
"So it's whoever did the most for these three criteria over the past year," he said.

He said Carney's name has likely been floated because of his resistance to Trump, along with the prime minister's efforts to strengthen ties with Europe — both seen as signs of international co-operation.
But Gjerløw pointed to other possible candidates, including the International Space Station.
"It would be a symbol of what we can achieve when we are able to co-operate as humanity," he said.

Gjerløw's other candidates include Mykola Kuleba and Save the Children, Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, the Committee to Protect Journalists, and the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.
Nobel Prize for physiology or medicine (Oct. 5.)
When The Scientist magazine asked its readers to suggest potential Nobel Prize winners in science, Canadian researcher Dr. Daniel Drucker was among the names put forward.

The endocrinologist won a 2025 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for discovering the GLP-1 hormone used in diabetes and obesity medications — including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro — that have changed the lives of millions of people around the world.
Prediction market Kalshi has also listed Drucker as one of the top contenders to win.
Nobel Prize for Literature (Oct. 8)

Another Canadian being discussed is poet and essayist Anne Carson, who has frequently been mentioned as a strong Nobel contender. Carson is a two-time winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize, and author of Autobiography of Red, Antigonick and Red Doc>.

However, one of Canada's most famous authors, Margaret Atwood, is also a contender according to Kalshi, but at lower odds. The Handmaid's Tale author has won two Booker prizes, and for years her name has been mentioned as a possible candidate for the Nobel Prize.
The last Canadian to win in this category was Alice Munro in 2013.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Gatchalian urges sleepyheads to watch impeachment trial at home
articles.summary: Prospective attendees who are sleep-deprived or too tired to attend the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should watch the proceedings at home instead of sleeping inside the Senate…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 3:48pm

Prospective attendees who are sleep-deprived or too tired to attend the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should watch the proceedings at home instead of sleeping inside the Senate session hall, Senate President and senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

“If they’re sleepy, they shouldn’t come. They can sleep at home and watch the proceedings on TV because it doesn’t look good to attend the impeachment court proceedings and then sleep there. They can just watch from home if they’re feeling sleepy,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.
Gatchalian made the statement after Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero called out Manila Rep. Bienvenido Abante for appearing to fall asleep during the trial.
Abante was seated in the VIP section of the Senate session hall when he fell asleep while Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña was testifying.

The House prosecution team called on the public to give Abante some leeway, saying it is normal for people of advanced age to feel sleepy at certain times of the day and that this does not make him any less of a dedicated public servant.
Senator-judge Ping Lacson also posted a photo of a sleeping Abante, saying he wondered where Abante would sleep that day, Sept. 30, after the impeachment trial was cancelled.

In a separate statement, Lacson said the prosecution had one-upped Duterte’s defense team because Abante and private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan had been caught sleeping, compared with former Chief Presidential Legal Counsel Salvador Panelo, who was on the defense side.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: PCG commended for vigilance vs Chinese research ship off Batanes
articles.summary: The National Maritime Council (NMC) commended on Sunday the Philippine Coast Guard"s (PCG) vigilance and continued monitoring of a Chinese research ship located within the country's exclusive…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 3:41pm

The National Maritime Council (NMC) commended on Sunday the Philippine Coast Guard’s (PCG) vigilance and continued monitoring of a Chinese research ship located within the country's exclusive economic zone (EEZ) off Itbayat, Batanes.
In a statement, the NMC described the Coast Guard’s response as a model of professionalism, vigilance, and restraint.

“The PCG’s response reflects an important principle of Philippine maritime governance: protecting our rights does not require unnecessary confrontation. It requires vigilance, sound judgment, professional conduct, and steadfast commitment to the rule of law,” the council said.

“... Through sustained monitoring and the deployment of BRP Teresa Magbanua (MRRV-9701), supported by maritime surveillance assets, the PCG demonstrated the Government’s resolve to protect Philippine maritime rights through coordinated, measured, and lawful action,” it added.
On September 28, the PCG reported spotting the Chinese research vessel JIA HAI KE 7 approximately 38 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat, well within the Philippines’ EEZ.

PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, stated that a PCG aircraft radio-challenged the vessel multiple times, asserting the Philippines' sovereign rights while advising the ship to declare its intentions and cease any unauthorized activities.
However, the Chinese vessel did not respond to the radio challenges.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) confirmed on Friday that the Chinese research is being conducted without the consent of the Philippines, which is required under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

“Under Article 246 of UNCLOS, marine scientific research in the EEZ and on the continental shelf shall be conducted with the consent of the coastal State. The Philippines did not receive any request from the Chinese side and no consent has been given to any Chinese vessel to conduct MSR,” DFA said.

The NMC said that it remains committed to reinforcing its maritime strategy, ensuring that any developments impacting national maritime interests are handled swiftly, consistently, and with proper regard for regional stability.
The Council called on China to immediately cease its unauthorized activities within Philippine waters and adhere to international law, including UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award.

“We call on China to stop the illegal and unauthorized activities of its vessels in the Philippines’ EEZ and abide by its obligations under UNCLOS, which include the obligation to comply with the 2016 Arbitral Award that upheld the Philippines’ sovereign rights and jurisdiction over marine scientific research in its EEZ,” the NMC said. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Conservatives claim ‘major victory’ as Tory conference begins after Labour scraps plans to curb jury trials – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Shadow justice secretary says despite U-turn Labour are still ‘restricting juries by the back door’, as Conservative conference begins in Birmingham

Good morning. Anthony…

blocks.text: Conservatives claim ‘major victory’ as Tory conference begins after Labour scraps plans to curb jury trials

Good morning. Anthony Seldon recently published the latest in his long and invaluable series of inside stories of premierships, Sunak at 10, and he gave it the subtitle “The last Conservative prime minister?” When the book was being planned in the early days of Kemi Badenoch’s leadership of the Conservative party, it did look as though the Tories might be finished as a party of government. But now Seldon, and his co-author Tom Egerton, aren’t so sure. Their book concludes: “At the time of writing in July 2026 … the Tory party still needs to engage in a process of deep self-reflection to understand why it failed in government, and tore itself so destructively apart, if it is ever to regain power. But at this point in time we believe it is unlikely that Sunak will have been the last Tory prime minister.”

That is a victory, of sorts, for Badenoch. For most of last year there were doubts that she would still be leader by the time of the next election. But she gave a successful party conference speech, her response to the budget was much admired, and her personal approval ratings with Tory members and right-leaning voters shot up. After two years as opposition leader, Iain Duncan Smith was booted out. Two years in, Badenoch’s position as leader is safe and it is even conceivable that she could stay on if the Conservatives were to lose the next election (in part because any Tories who favour a radically different policy approach are being purged from the candidates list).

But that does not mean Badenoch’s leadership is going well. At the last election the Conservatives won 24.4% of the GB vote. According to the Politico poll of polls, they have been consistently polling below that since the end of 2024 and they are currently on 19%.

The Conservative conference starts today and, explaining her strategy in an interview in the Times, Badenoch said: “Last year was about telling the party who I was. Now the party is going to be showing the country who we are: a strong team of people who actually like each other.” The Tories have already announced quite a lot of conference-related policy.

But she has not got the news space all to herself. It is the final day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton and this morning activists are expected to debate their ‘Zionism is racism’ motion. The proposal has split the party, and critics claim that it is antisemitic. Whatever happens, it will affect how the Green party is seen.
And this morning Labour has announced a major U-turn – abandoning most of the Keir Starmer/David Lammy plans to restrict access to jury trials. Haroon Siddique has the story here.

In the past, there was an unofficial ‘gentleman’s agreement’ that the government did not make big news announcements during the opposition party’s conference. But that era (like two-party politics) is over, and Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has successfully kept Badenoch off the top of this morning’s news cycle.
Still, the Tories can claim this as a victory. This is from Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary.

double quotation markThis is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour has been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the crown court.
But Timothy also claimed the U-turn did not go far enough.

double quotation markLabour are restricting juries by the back door, scrapping the right to elect one and dumping those cases on magistrates whose backlog is at a record high. Nearly 81,000 cases are stuck in the crown court, yet there is no commitment to get courts sitting more often, but Labour did find the time to write into law a review of how its reforms treat people of different backgrounds.
Here is the agenda for the day.
8.30am: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, is interviewed on Sky’s Sunday with Helen Lewis.
9am: Kemi Badenoch is interviewed on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. (The interview has been pre-recorded.) Norris is being interviewed too.
Morning: The Green party debates the controversial ‘Zionism is racism’ motion on the final day of its conference this morning.

2pm: John Belsley, president of the National Conservative Convention, opens the proceedings at the Tory conference in Birmingham. The session is on the theme of “resisting separatism” and the speakers include Alex Burghart, the deputy leader and shadow Northern Ireland secretary; Mims Davies, shadow Welsh secretary; Harriet Cross, shadow Scottish secretary; Darren Millar, leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd; and Russell Findlay, the Scottish leader.
Mid afternoon: Badenoch delivers her opening speech to the conference.
4pm: James Cleverly, who wants to be the Tory candidate for London mayor in 2028, is speaking at a fringe event.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Constant oil price hikes enough reason to suspend fuel excise tax - Win Gatchalian
articles.summary: The continuous increase in oil prices should be sufficient reason to temporarily suspend the excise tax on gasoline and diesel, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 3:09pm
The continuous increase in oil prices should be sufficient reason to temporarily suspend the excise tax on gasoline and diesel, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

“Dapat suspendihin na 'yan dahil ang gumagamit din ng diesel, gasolina ay logistics company, at ‘yan ay ipinapasa sa pagkain. Noon pa man, ang mungkahi natin ay i-suspend na rin ang gasolina, para makatulong sa pagbaba ng presyo ng mga bilihin at hindi na maipasa pa sa iba pang pangunahing bilihin,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.

(The [excise tax] should already be suspended because diesel and gasoline are also used by logistics companies, and the cost is passed on to food prices. Even before, we had already proposed suspending the excise tax on gasoline to help bring down the prices of goods and prevent the cost from being passed on to other basic commodities.)

“Dapat i-reconsider nila (economic managers) ‘yang pag suspinde rin sa excise tax sa gasolina at diesel. Dapat i-reconsider ng economic managers nation kanit temporary lang dahil umabot na ulit sa more than $80 barrel at tuloy-tuloy. Mayroon nang dahilan para suspendinin,” he added.

(The economic managers should reconsider suspending the excise tax on gasoline and diesel, even if only temporarily, because oil prices have risen above $80 a barrel again and continue to climb. There is now sufficient reason to suspend it.)
In September, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered the suspension of the collection of excise tax on liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and kerosene.
Marcos issued Executive Order No. 125 amid soaring global crude oil prices, which drove local petroleum prices to high levels.

According to Executive Order No. 125, "The excise taxes on LPG, except when used as raw material for production of petrochemical products or used for motive power, and kerosene, except when used as aviation fuel, are hereby fully suspended."
Marcos signed Republic Act 12316 into law in March, giving him emergency powers to suspend or reduce the excise tax rate on fuel.

Under the measure, the suspension or reduction may be implemented for up to three months if the average price of Dubai crude oil —based on the Mean of Platts Singapore (MOPS)—reaches or exceeds $80 per barrel for one month. Brent crude prices have hovered around $102 per barrel.
In a separate dzBB interview, Department of Energy Oil Industry Management Bureau Director Rino Abad said the following estimated fuel price adjustments are expected next week:

items: Gasoline - P1.50 per liter increase
Kerosene - P2 per liter increase
Diesel - P1 per liter decrease

articles.title: JV Ejercito bill seeks to double indigent seniors' pension to P2,000
articles.summary: Senator JV Ejercito has filed a bill seeking to double the monthly social pension for indigent senior citizens from P1,000 to P2,000 amid rising prices of goods and other basic needs.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 2:57pm
Senator JV Ejercito has filed a bill seeking to double the monthly social pension for indigent senior citizens from P1,000 to P2,000 amid rising prices of goods and other basic needs.
Senate Bill No. 2522 seeks to amend Republic Act No. 11916, which doubled the monthly social pension from P500 to the current P1,000.
Ejercito said the P1,000 monthly pension is no longer enough to cover the needs and expenses of senior citizens.

“Seniors should not be forced to choose between buying medicine and buying food. Their lifetime of work and sacrifices should not end in anxiety over whether there will be enough money for the next meal or the next prescription,” Ejercito said in the bill’s explanatory note.
“Social pension is not charity. Ultimately, this measure is about how we value those who came before us,” he added.

The proposed measure would expand the definition of an indigent senior citizen to include those with no regular income or pension, as well as retirees receiving pensions or financial assistance of P10,000 or less per month, as determined by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).
The bill would also remove the existing requirement that an indigent senior citizen be frail, sickly or disabled to qualify for the pension.

Moreover, the bill would require the DSWD, with the approval of the Department of Budget and Management and after consulting stakeholders, to review and adjust the social pension amount every two years based on economic indicators such as the consumer price index and cost of living.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Impeachment court may rule on Sara Duterte case by end-November --Sen. Gatchalian
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court is targeting to issue its ruling on Vice President Sara Duterte"s case by the end of November, Senate President and senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 2:26pm
The Senate impeachment court is targeting to issue its ruling on Vice President Sara Duterte’s case by the end of November, Senate President and senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

“Ako personally, baka we need mga 30 to 45 days from now... Ang isyu lang, magkakaroon kami ng 2-week break sa end of October. Hopefully within 30 to 45 days (calendar days),” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.
(I personally think we may need 30 to 45 days from now. The only issue is that we will have a two-week break at the end of October. Hopefully, within 30 to 45 calendar days.)
“Siguro mga mid-November to end of November [posibleng matapos ang impeachment trial at makapaghatol kay VP Duterte]. Tingin ko,” he added.
(Maybe by mid-November to the end of November, the impeachment trial could be completed, and a verdict could be handed down on VP Duterte.)
Gatchalian further said the goal is to finish the impeachment proceedings before Christmas, but recent changes may allow them to wrap up sooner.
“Marami kasing pagbabago. Una sa lahat, bumilis... Pangalawa, maraming testigo ang tinanggal at nagbigay ng mas mahabang oras ang impeachment court,” he said.
(There have been many changes. First, the proceedings have moved faster. Second, several witnesses were dropped, and the impeachment court gave us more time.)
The Senate impeachment court is currently tackling Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment on the unexplained wealth of Duterte.
In a separate dzBB interview, House trial spokesperson Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said the prosecution team is considering dropping the bribery charges against Duterte.

"Mukhang ang direction is hindi na siya ita-tackle. Maybe that's the direction pero hindi pa natin pina-finalize 'yan kasi ongoing pa rin ang discussion sa prosecution panel kung anong magiging susunod na hakbang pagkatapos ng Article 2," Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.

(It appears that it will no longer be tackled. That may be the direction, but we have not finalized it yet because discussions are still ongoing among the prosecution panel on what the next steps will be after Article 2.)
Adiong then confirmed when asked whether the decision was because the first three impeachment articles were already strong enough to convict Duterte.
Article 3 accuses the Vice President of bribing officials of the Department of Education during her stint as DepEd secretary from 2022 to 2024. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
articles.summary: State police and the country's security agency are looking into the co-pilot, who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel.

blocks.text: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.
The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.
The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.
The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.
In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".
The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".

Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.
Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel.
Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.

The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.
Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar, and Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.
The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.
He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.
In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.

While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.
It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.
He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

articles.title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets
articles.summary:
Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures

Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China…

blocks.text: Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposes duties of up to 45%.

EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China.

Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.

“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.

“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.

Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.

The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
after newsletter promotion

Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”

Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”

He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

articles.title: After Trump’s Venezuelan oil deal, those living on polluted lake in oil country wait for change
articles.summary: In late August, the U.S. signed a sweeping oil deal with Venezuela's interim authorities to control a share of the country's oil. In one of the largest oil-producing regions, residents welcome…

image.caption: The shore of Lake Maracaibo from above. Fishing communities who live by the water say frequent oil spills on the lake have affected their health and their livelihoods. (Camille Rodríguez Montilla)

blocks.text: World

In late August, the U.S. signed a sweeping oil deal with Venezuela's interim authorities to control a share of the country's oil. In one of the largest oil-producing regions, residents welcome promises to revitalize the industry, they also have a more immediate demand: clean up the polluted lake.
Lake Maracaibo has become a symbol of the deteriorated state of the Venezuela's oil industry
Jessica Partida, 42, needs a $30 US ultrasound for her kidneys, which she can’t afford.

Her husband, Enrique Olivares, fishes on Lake Maracaibo, and for days the oil in the water has prevented him from catching the shrimp he uses as bait. Without bait, he cannot fish, and when he doesn’t fish, he doesn’t make money.
“I left the hospital because my husband hasn’t been able to fish because of the oil,” she said.

Partida’s family of six lives in a block home in Cabimas, about 500 km west of Caracas, on the shore of one of the country’s largest oil-producing regions. Just over a century ago, a Royal Dutch Shell subsidiary first struck oil here. The lake (technically an estuary) served as a symbol for Venezuela’s oil wealth for decades.

But today, the water is dotted with rusting rigs and pumpjacks. Most of them are out of use and some leak oil and gas into the water. Now, the lake that once embodied Venezuela’s oil bonanza has come to symbolize the industry’s collapse.

Venezuela holds the largest proven oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels, but accounts for only about one per cent of global supply. Oil output has fallen by about two-thirds since the early 2000s.

The decline began under former president Hugo Chávez, when state oil company PDVSA fired around 18,000 skilled workers following a 2002-2003 strike. Revenues were diverted away from maintenance, and much of the oil infrastructure has been left to decay. U.S. sanctions imposed in 2017 and 2019 compounded the problems.
“We don’t feel the oil wealth,” Partida said. “We don’t sell the oil, we don’t do anything with it. It just sits there, going to waste.”

Oil fields in the Maracaibo Basin, where the lake is located, are part of the sweeping energy deal reached in late August between the United States and Venezuela’s interim authorities. It grants private company North American Blue Energy Partners a 100-year concession over 17 oil fields around the country. The company has promised to double oil production in two years.
While many in the community surrounding the lake welcome promises to revitalize the oil sector, they also have a more immediate demand: clean up the polluted lake.
Fishing despite spills

The oil shifts with winds and currents, but fishermen say it often drifts toward them in the early afternoon, just when they would normally head out to collect shrimp to use as bait for the following morning.

“When there’s a lot of oil, we don’t do anything,” said Gregory Díaz, 36, who has fished the lake for 20 years. “When we throw our nets, they become covered in oil, and if the nets get damaged, we have nothing to work with.”

“The oil companies used to come clean the shore but stopped,” said Olivares, who has fished on the lake for over a decade. “Used to, PDVSA would replace our nets when they were damaged, but they haven’t done that in years.”

Data on oil spills in Venezuela are outdated. The Observatory of Political Ecology of Venezuela, which tracks pollution events across the country, counted more than 80 oil spills in 2022, the last year for which figures are available. Most were located in the western part of the country near the lake.
Those who live along the lake say the spills haven’t stopped, and many describe dozens of large ones each year.

“This one just exploded a few weeks ago,” said Carlos Rodríguez from his fishing boat as he steered toward a pumpjack that was leaking gas and covered in sticky crude, which was also dripping into the water. There was a heavy smell of gas for several metres around the machine.
The crude oil covers every surface in contact with the water, leaving a black slimy residue.
Many say the constant smell and contact with the oil has impacted their health.
“There are people who suffer from asthma and it chokes them,” said Rodríguez. “Most have left because the oil chokes them so much and they would rather live somewhere else.”
“The kids go swimming and come out stained with oil,” Partida said.
No cleanup scheduled

Neither the U.S. nor Venezuelan authorities have mentioned cleanup of the lake as part of the new oil deal. Venezuelan authorities have made several unfulfilled promises in recent years to clean up the water and shore, most recently in 2023, when the Environmental Ministry promised a “national team” to clean 600 beaches by the lake.
The government’s communication ministry didn’t respond to a request for comment.

items: The U.S. could soon control 20% of Venezuela's oil reserves. Canada's oilpatch isn't worried
Venezuelans of all stripes are denouncing Trump's 'biggest oil deal ever'

blocks.text: One local environmental organization, Azul Ambientalistas, has demanded that five per cent of revenue from new oil output go to efforts to clean the lake.
Cleaning up the lake is the first thing many residents want, so they can fish. But many say they would also welcome the chance to work with the oil, instead of only alongside it.
“If they call me, I’ll go to work,” Olivares said.
So far, he says they haven’t felt any economic change since the new oil deal was announced.
Díaz, who has two daughters, ages five and seven, says a job on land “could change your life.”
“Here we depend on fishing. If we catch something, we eat. If we don’t, we don’t have money,” he said.
Their catches have dwindled by 40 per cent in recent years due to the oil in the water, he estimates.

Some residents say a company recently came through the neighbourhood collecting names, phone numbers and addresses should new jobs open up. Olivares says he is on the list, but so far no one has called.
For Partida, the ultrasound of her kidneys will have to wait until her family’s economic situation improves. She says she’s hopeful the new oil money will soon be felt.
“I believe it, but sometimes I have doubts, because time passes and there are still gas leaks and oil spills,” she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Cody Weddle is a journalist covering Latin America from Bogotá, Colombia. He has focused on the region for nearly a decade, including five years living in and reporting on Venezuela.

articles.title: Prosecution likely to drop bribery charges in VP Sara Duterte impeachment --Adiong
articles.summary: The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is likely to drop the bribery charges against her, House prosecution spokesperson Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 12:59pm

The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is likely to drop the bribery charges against her, House prosecution spokesperson and Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said Sunday.

"Mukhang ang direction is hindi na siya ita-tackle. Maybe that's the direction pero hindi pa natin pina-finalize 'yan kasi ongoing pa rin ang discussion sa prosecution panel kung anong magiging susunod na hakbang pagkatapos ng Article 2," Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.

(It appears that it will no longer be tackled. That may be the direction, but we have not finalized it yet because discussions are still ongoing among the prosecution panel on what the next steps will be after Article 2.)
When asked whether the decision was because the first three impeachment articles were already strong enough to convict Duterte, Adiong confirmed.
"That's one way of looking at it kasi bakit mo pa papahabain 'yung trial kung para sa amin naman ay napakita namin 'yung mga kinakailangan na ebidensiya," Adiong said.
(That is one way of looking at it because why prolong the trial if, in our view, we have already presented the necessary evidence.)

"Kasi unang-una, hindi lang role ng prosecution... hindi lang to make sure may trial o may pagkakataong magpresenta ng ebidensiya. Ultimately, ang sini-seek natin dito is justice, justice para sa taongbayan," he added.

(Because, first and foremost, the role of the prosecution is not merely to ensure that there is a trial or an opportunity to present evidence. Ultimately, what we are seeking here is justice for the Filipinos.)
The Senate Impeachment Court is currently tackling Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment on unexplained wealth of Duterte.
Meanwhile, Article 3 accuses the Vice President of bribing officials of the Department of Education during her stint as DepEd secretary from 2022 to 2024. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Polls suggest the election will be a closely run contest between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing rival.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP
The two candidates leading in the polls are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro
ByVanessa Buschschlüter
Latin America online editor
Brazilians are voting on Sunday in a general election in which the two front-runners for the presidency bear very familiar names.
The incumbent, veteran left-wing leader Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva, will be challenged by 11 candidates, the most prominent of whom is right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro.

In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father Jair, but the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.
Here's what you need to know.
The man not on the ballot

blocks.caption: Image caption, At the launch of his campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro screened a video in which an AI-generated image of his father endorsed his candidacy

blocks.text: Image source, Nelson ALMEIDA / AFP via Getty Images
At the launch of his campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro screened a video in which an AI-generated image of his father endorsed his candidacy
Jair Bolsonaro, the right-wing former army captain who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2023, will not be running for president in this election.
Not only is the 71-year-old barred from standing for office, he is also serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Due to recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has had restrictions imposed on him prohibiting him from posting on social media or making public statements.
Despite these restrictions, his shadow - and sometimes his moving and talking image - looms large over this election.
At the event where Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his presidential campaign, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsed his son's candidacy.

When pressed by the Supreme Court about the deepfake, Jair Bolsonaro's lawyers may have denied he had given his permission for its use, but there is nevertheless little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has the backing of his father.
What do the polls say?
While there are 12 candidates running for the presidency, there are only two who have reached double figures in the opinion polls, and they are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro.
BBC Brasil's poll tracker shows them both hovering around the 40% mark, with Lula slightly ahead of Bolsonaro.
The other 11 candidates are polling at 4% or less.
If none of the candidates gains 50% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off election on 25 October.
The opinion polls suggest a run-off is highly likely - but with a relatively high number of voters still undecided just days before the election, an outright win cannot be entirely ruled out.
BBC Brasil's poll aggregator suggests that at the end of September, 9% of voters were either still undecided, or planning to spoil their ballot, cast a blank ballot or not go to the polls at all.
Brazilians who are 16 years of age or older are entitled to vote and it is compulsory for those aged between 18 and 70 who are literate, with a fine imposed on those who do not cast a ballot.

Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this election and, with polls typically surveying just thousands of people, the end result can differ considerably from the indications given by surveys.
What does Lula stand for?

blocks.caption: Image caption, In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Lula stressed his country's sovereignty

blocks.text: Image source, Olga Fedorova/EPA/Shutterstock
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Lula stressed his country's sovereignty
Lula, the 80-year-old candidate for the left-wing Workers' Party, has been president three times already.

He served two consecutive terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - and was widely praised for lifting millions out of poverty during this time with the help of a cash-transfer programme called Bolsa Família.
The former metalworker left office with record approval ratings of over 80%, but his party was later rocked by huge corruption scandals.
Lula himself spent more than 18 months in prison between 2018 and 2019 after being convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he has always denied.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points.
When he started his third term in office, he vowed it would be his last, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 later this month.

There is no doubt he remains a towering figure in the left. But while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
During Lula's latest term in office, relations with his US counterpart Donald Trump have been rocky.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

In another thinly veiled reference to both his rival Flávio Bolsonaro and those in the Trump administration who would like to see the right-wing candidate win, the Brazilian leader has also warned that he would not tolerate "foreign and local enemies of democracy" interfering with the polls.
What is Bolsonaro promising?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Flávio Bolsonaro has been courting his father's supporters

blocks.text: Image source, Adriano Machado/Reuters
Flávio Bolsonaro has been courting his father's supporters
Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is Jair Bolsonaro's eldest son and has been serving as a senator since 2019.

The younger Bolsonaro is running for the right-wing Liberal Party (PL) and, while he is widely seen as less confrontational than his father, he is appealing to the followers of the older Bolsonaro by promising to broadly continue in his footsteps.

During his time in the Senate, the trained lawyer has advocated a tough-on-crime stance, calling for longer sentences and laxer gun laws, arguing that "decent citizens" should be able to defend themselves from criminals.

He has successfully lobbied for the US to declare Brazil-based criminal gangs Comando Vermelho (CV) and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, a move that was opposed by Lula.
The younger Bolsonaro has also courted evangelicals and the agricultural industry as part of his campaign.
He has said that he will cut what he says are unnecessary regulations and "get the state off farmers' backs".

Quizzed in an interview with Globo in August on whether he still believed - as he had said in 2019 - that climate change did not exist, he acknowledged that there had been "extreme climate events", but insisted that these events were "cyclical".
Flávio Bolsonaro has actively courted Trump and members of his administration by portraying himself as a loyal ally during a meeting at the White House in May.
More recently, he promised to join the US-led anti-crime alliance that the Trump administration has dubbed "Shield of the Americas", should he be elected.
What are the main issues worrying voters?
Up until a few months ago, Brazilians told pollsters that crime and security were their main concerns.
But in the weeks leading up to the election, a scandal involving a jailed banker accused of orchestrating one of Brazil's largest financial fraud cases has pushed corruption to the top of the list.
The banker, Daniel Vorcaro, is well connected and has ties to many powerful people in Brazil - both on the political right and left.
Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged asking Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).
Police have since then opened an investigation into Flávio Bolsonaro for suspected corruption and money laundering over the financing of the film.
But pollsters say Lula's campaign was also hurt by the Vorcaro scandal, after alleged links emerged between the disgraced banker and an ally of Lula, the Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.
Moraes is the man who presided over Jair Bolsonaro's trial and has made a number of subsequent rulings about the conditions of his detention.
A police report suggested that Vorcaro had made numerous calls and sent a number of messages to a phone number which officers say is linked to Moraes.
The investigators say Vorcaro asked the person with whom he was communicating for help avoiding arrest.

Moraes has denied any wrongdoing but these latest revelations mean that, in the crucial weeks before the election, attention shifted away from the allegations against Flávio Bolsonaro to those against the Supreme Court justice.
Lula has tried to distance himself from Moraes, saying that "no one is above the law", but his rival has already pounced on the allegations against the judge to make political hay.
"Voting for Lula means voting for Moraes," Flávio Bolsonaro told his supporters at a rally, using the right's intense dislike of the judge to shore up his own support.

articles.title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
articles.summary: Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.

image.caption: Rebel groups had seized control of airports and sections of Tigray's capital on September 23Image: AFP

blocks.text: Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022.
Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle.
"The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity.
The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in.
Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access.
Return to civil war?
Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict

The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president.
The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September.

The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week.
Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020.
The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.
Fears of wider regional unrest
The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region, with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa.
For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this.
Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties, with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies.
The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint.
Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea
The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea."

articles.title: No bail for P-plater over Newcastle crash that left five-year-old in induced coma and injured nine other NRL fans
articles.summary:
Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, appears in court on dangerous driving offences after car struck Knights supporters lining streets to farewell their team

  • Get our
articles.byline: Australian Associated Press and Andrew Messenger

blocks.text: A driver whose car careered into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters – leaving children as young as five injured – will be kept in custody as the community rallies to support those hospitalised after the crash.
Ten people were left injured after a car allegedly driven by 18-year-old P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe careered into the crowd near a major roundabout on Saturday morning.

Six people remain at the John Hunter hospital with injuries caused by the collision, according to the Hunter New England Local Health District chief executive, Tracey McCosker. Two are in a serious condition, while four are stable.
They include a five-year-old girl who had been placed into an induced coma with critical injuries, although her condition has stabilised.

Samarasinghe was taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences, including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.
He did not make any application for release during a brief court appearance on Sunday, and he was formally refused bail. The judge also endorsed a warrant for a health assessment.
The bail court was told the most serious offence of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm carried a maximum jail term of seven years.
He will next appear at the Newcastle local court on 15 October.

Chris Clancy was among those injured in the crash, after joining thousands of Newcastle Knights fans to lined the streets to farewell their team as the players travelled to Sydney for the grand final.
“We’re there at the roundabout having fun – cars going past, beeping their horns, people waving,” Clancy said.
“The next thing, this car stops [at] the roundabout and then he just floored it on the wet ground, lost it.
“It happened in seconds, but when you stand there, seeing the car coming at you, I honestly thought I was going to die. It just felt like slow motion.”
Clancy suffered small fractures in his ribs and spine, a broken collarbone, and small fractures in his foot.
after newsletter promotion
Investigators did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was being driven erratically before the crash.
Multiple fundraisers have been established for the victims of the incident, including one for the five-year-old girl and another for Wallsend grandfather Dave Martin.
Martin was injured after being struck by the car while trying to protect his two young granddaughters, sustaining multiple fractures in both legs and undergoing a lengthy surgery.
He was known in Wallsend for his love of the Knights, often decorating his barber shop on Nelson Street with team paraphernalia.
The Knights’ chief executive, Peter Parr, expressed deep concern for those affected by the crash.
“Newcastle is a strong community,” he said.
“We have seen that strength throughout this week, and today we need to draw on it again with compassion, care and support for those who need it most.”

articles.title: DSWD provides parenting effectiveness service amid school violence incidents
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development is providing parenting effectiveness service to families amid the recent school violence incidents across the country.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 11:26am
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is providing parenting effectiveness service to families amid the recent school violence incidents across the country.
DSWD spokesperson Irene Dumlao said the service will strengthen parents in their parental responsibilities.

"Ang mahalaga dito ay 'yung na pro-provide na parenting effectiveness service para mas mapalakas pa ang ugnayan ng pamilya, and for the parents na mapalakas 'yung pag-perform nila ng parental responsibilities," Dumlao told Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday.
(What's important is that the parenting effectiveness service can help strengthen the relationships in a family and the parents' capabilities to perform their parental responsibilities.)

"Ibig sabihin, sa loob ng tahanan, napakalakas na ang ugnayan at ang relasyon para magabayan nang magabayan nang husto ng mga magulang ang kanilang mga anak ng sa gayon mailayo sila sa kapahamakan o karahasan," she added
(This means strengthening relationships and communication within the home so that parents can properly guide their children, help them make better decisions, and protect them from harm or violence.)
A Grade 11 student was wounded after being stabbed by a fellow student at a school in Laoag City on Friday. The incident involved teenagers believed to have a confrontation.
In June, two students opened fire on their classmates at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, killing three students and injuring 20 others.
In August, a student shot his classmate at Ateneo de Zamboanga University before turning the gun on himself, leading to two deaths.
Dumlao shared that DSWD also provides psychosocial first aid to affected individuals who have witnessed incidents of violence.
The agency also provides capacity building for trauma care so that other individuals in the school can observe the behaviors of affected people.
Dumlao said DSWD's social workers are assessing affected families to determine what assistance the department will provide. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Peru: Fire burning on road to Machu Picchu kills 1
articles.summary: One person has died and two others have suffered burns in a fire near the main access route to the historic sanctuary of Machu Picchu.

image.caption: The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century Image: Laurent Davoust/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: A blaze was burning near the main access road to the ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu in Peru, leaving one person dead and two injured, officials said on Saturday.
The fire began on Friday in the Sacred Valley of the Cusco region, which also includes the Ollantaytambo train station — the busiest for travelers visiting Machu Picchu.
"We have one elderly person who died in the flames and two others with second-degree burns," Miguel Osco, head of the Cusco Regional Office for Disaster Management and Safety, told RPP radio.
How did the fire start?
Osco said the fire originated from controlled bush burning that farmers carry out to clear land for crops.
The flames spread quickly because of the hot, windy weather and dry vegetation, he added.
The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century.
Located at an altitude of 2,500 meters in the Andes Mountains, the historic sanctuary is regarded as an architectural masterpiece.
UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983.
Machu Picchu is Peru's most famous tourist destination, attracting about three million visitors every year.

articles.title: Chalmers says global economic turmoil will drive budget cuts, but Australia should avoid recession
articles.summary:
Treasurer says ‘very substantial and intensifying pressure’ on federal budget as he points finger at private sector for driving up inflation amid Middle East conflict

  • Get our

blocks.text: Jim Chalmers has warned of “very substantial and intensifying” economic pressures on the horizon but insists he’s not planning for a recession, as he prepares to find new ways to cut the budget ahead of its mid-year update.

The treasurer on Sunday called on critics of government spending to name the services that should be cut, as he points the finger at the private sector for driving up inflation in Australia amid the protracted conflict in the Middle East.
Chalmers said the US-led eight-month war against Iran, which has severely curtailed global oil supplies from the region, has been “disastrous” for cost-of-living pressures.
He also said there was “very substantial and intensifying pressure” on the federal budget.

“No serious observer of what’s going on right now would conclude anything other than [that],” he told ABC’s Insiders. “The longer this thing drags out, the bigger the impact on the global economy and on the Australian economy, whether it’s … on inflation or downward pressure on growth.
“We’re not anticipating [a recession] here in Australia, but certainly it is weighing on global growth, and we’re not immune from that.”
Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, while the Reserve Bank lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, the highest figure since 2011.

Chalmers said the government was working on finding further savings to the budget in the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook, due in December, after cuts of $44.9bn over four years were identified in the May budget.
The treasurer said cuts to government spending weren’t the only factor driving up inflation in the economy, and cutting larger sums would impact essential services.

“If people don’t want us to strengthen Medicare, for example, or cut income taxes, or provide cost-of-living relief in other ways, then they should nominate where that should be cut,” he said on Sunday.
Beyond the war’s impact on driving up prices in Australia, Chalmers said the private sector was partly to blame.
“For every $5 of demand in our economy, $1 is public, $4 is private,” he said.
“Budget settings are not the primary driver of prices in our economy. There’s a whole bunch of other things going on.”
after newsletter promotion
But the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said Chalmers should be sacked, claiming his decisions have increased inflation to generate tax windfalls.

“He’s actively stoked inflation, and he’s fundamentally undermined the success of this country, and now he’s announced today he’s on a sort of Argo-style salvation trip for investment, because he’s created a problem of sovereign risk,” he told News24.
The assistant science and digital technology minister, Andrew Charlton, said the consequences of having a recession, which would ease inflation, would be devastating.
“If you have a recession, you throw hundreds of thousands of people on to the unemployment queues, and that pulls a huge amount of demand out of the economy,” he told News24.
“It’s pretty easy to have low interest rates and low inflation if your economy goes through a recession.
“As a Labor government, that is a big priority for us to make sure that we don’t go into a recession that drives a lot of people into unemployment.”
Chalmers will travel to Japan for meetings with business leaders and the country’s finance minister, in an effort to boost investment and improve fuel security.
